articles.title: Ukraine war latest: 'Russia's mass murder' — Deadly Russian strikes on Dnipro, Chernihiv, Kremenchuk
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: 'Russia's mass murder' — Deadly Russian strikes on Dnipro, Chernihiv, Kremenchuk
Key developments on Oct. 28:
- 'Russia's mass murder:' Drone strike on Dnipro station kills 14 amid deadly daytime attacks on Chernihiv, Kremenchuk
- Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
- Route demining completed in Russian-occupied Oleshky as humanitarian convoy prepares to enter, Ukraine's ombudsman says
- Ukraine strikes Russian 'drone port' in Bryansk Oblast, damaging storage facilities, military says
- UN appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action, as Ukraine clears over 300,000 explosives in Kherson Oblast
- Russian general charged in absentia for missile strike on museum dedicated to 18th century Ukrainian philosopher
Russian forces struck a train platform at Dnipro railway station on the morning of Oct. 29, killing at least 14 people and wounding at least 14 more, authorities said.
A passenger train was preparing to depart the platform for Zaporizhzhia when the station was attacked by a Russian jet-powered drone, Ukrainian Railways wrote on social media.
The brazen daytime attack was followed in close succession by deadly strikes against civilians in Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.
The strikes on civilians come not only in the middle of a scheduled local ceasefire in Kherson Oblast, agreed to by Kyiv and Moscow to help evacuate and deliver aid to the residents of the occupied city of Oleshky, but also ahead of the first trilateral "peace negotiations" mediated by the United States since February this year.
According to Ukraine's Air Force, Dnipro was attacked around 11:00 a.m. by four Russian jet-powered drones, three of which were downed by Ukrainian air defense before reaching their targets.
Despite the air raid alert and announcements of a heightened threat, people remained on the platform, Ukrainian Railways said.
Passengers were told to evacuate from the stationary train around ten minutes before the strike, with station and train staff checking each train car one by one.
At 11:29 a.m., Dnipropetrovsk Oblast governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported that medics were already at the scene of the attack, providing first aid.
"A horrific Russian attack on Dnipro train station," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media in response to the attack. "The Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
"How many such terrorist attacks has Russia carried out on our people after lifting sanctions on some Russian oligarchs and energy companies instead of de-escalating."
Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze described the attack on Dnipro as "mass murder."
Following the Russian attack on Dnipro, 25,000 people in the city and surrounding Oblast were left without electricity, Hanzha said in the afternoon.
Later in the day, Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov reported that a Russian drone struck the dormitory of a vocational school in Dnipro, setting the entire fifth floor on fire. There were no injuries, Filatov said, as the students had managed to reach the shelter before the strike.
Throughout the day, Russian attacks across Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured four more people, including a 15-year-old girl, Hanzha said in an evening statement.
Elsewhere across Ukraine, the cities of Chernihiv and Kremenchuk were also targeted by daytime Russian attacks.
Around noon, Russian forces struck the center of Chernihiv in northern Ukraine with Banderol cruise missiles, killing two 15-year-old girls, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
At least 25 more people were injured in the attack, including four children, the youngest one 10-months-old, Chaus later said.
Meanwhile, in the city of Kremenchuk in Poltava Oblast, at least three people were killed and 32 injured, including six children and two people still in critical condition, after Russian drones struck an apartment building in a residential area, according to local authorities. Oct. 30 has been declared a day of mourning in Poltava Oblast.

Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
Ukraine's Navy destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets in a strike against the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast, using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported on Oct. 29.
The aircraft were destroyed at the base of Russia's 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment near the settlement of Oktyabrsky, according to the Navy. The regiment belongs to the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of Russia's 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army. The Navy did not provide any visual confirmation of the strike. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
Later on Oct. 29, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the destruction of the two Su-34 jets, adding that Ukrainian forces had also hit a Russian Iskander missile launcher.
The Su-34 is one of Russia's main aircraft used to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, frontline settlements, and military positions. Strikes against these aircraft could weaken Russia's ability to carry out such attacks, while replacing the losses requires significant time and resources.
Russia had approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service as of Oct. 22, including the modernized Su-34M, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) reported on Oct. 29.
According to the agency, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed and another seven damaged since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Such losses are quite significant for the aggressor's aircraft fleet, whose restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation," HUR said.
The agency estimated that Russia can manufacture approximately 14 to 18 Su-34 aircraft annually, meaning the number of destroyed aircraft is equivalent to roughly 2.5–3 years of production.

Route demining completed in Russian-occupied Oleshky as humanitarian convoy prepares to enter, Ukraine's ombudsman says
Demining of designated routes in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has been completed, and a humanitarian convoy is ready to depart, Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets announced on Oct. 29.
The convoy is expected to arrive at the city's central hospital, where humanitarian assistance will be provided to residents, Lubinets said.
Residents wishing to leave the city will be able to do so until 2:00 p.m. local time, with security measures arranged for their evacuation. Humanitarian aid distribution is scheduled to begin after 2:30 p.m., according to the ombudsman.
Delegations from Ukraine, Russia, and the United States have gathered to coordinate the next steps of the mission, with journalists from all three countries also present, Lubinets said.
The mission is being carried out jointly with Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova, with mediation and coordination by U.S. first lady Melania Trump.
"Our shared goal is to deliver humanitarian aid to civilians and facilitate the safe departure of everyone who wishes to leave the city," Lubinets said.
The operation follows a temporary ceasefire in and around Oleshky, announced by the White House on Oct. 23 and subsequently confirmed by Ukraine and Russia. The pause in fighting, which began on Oct. 27, is expected to remain in effect until Nov. 1 to allow aid deliveries, mine clearance, and civilian evacuations.

Ukraine strikes Russian 'drone port' in Bryansk Oblast, damaging storage facilities, military says
Ukrainian forces have struck a Russian military facility used to launch long-range attack drones at Ukraine, the General Staff said on Oct. 29.
The overnight attack targeted the Russian drone base near Navlya in Bryansk Oblast, around 70 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
According to the General Staff, the strikes damaged a storage facility for Russian long-range Geran-type drones, as well as fuel and lubricant storage facilities and the 'drone port' itself.
Ukrainian media and open-source intelligence (OSINT) groups have tracked Russia's building of several large 'airfields' designed for unmanned systems and built across Russia's western border areas.
The building of these new 'drone ports' reflects Moscow's growing investment in long-range attack drones as a long-term strategic tool, which can be used both against Ukraine or against countries on NATO's eastern flank.
The Oct. 29 attack was the second strike on the Navlya facility, with the first being on Aug. 3, also targeting launch and storage facilities.

UN appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action, as Ukraine clears over 300,000 explosives in Kherson Oblast
The United Nations has appointed a Russian diplomat to a senior position overseeing mine action, drawing criticism from Ukraine as the country continues to clear hundreds of thousands of explosive devices left behind by Russia's war.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres announced the appointment of Gleb Desyatnikov as assistant secretary-general for mine action and police in the Department of Peace Operations on Oct. 27.
Desyatnikov has served as Russia's ambassador to Jordan since 2018, including throughout Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to the U.N., he has more than 35 years of experience in international relations and security affairs, including previous positions at Russia's Foreign Ministry.
"Moscow has mined the United Nations," Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi wrote on X on Oct. 29, criticizing the decision.
"Entrusting this responsibility to a representative of the aggressor state is deeply troubling and undermines trust in the United Nations," he added.
The appointment comes as Ukraine faces one of the world's largest demining challenges, with Russian mines and unexploded ordnance threatening civilians and complicating the recovery of agricultural land and infrastructure.
In southern Kherson Oblast, demining teams have neutralized 300,691 explosive devices on the Ukrainian-controlled right bank since the start of clearance operations, according to the regional military administration.
Between Oct. 22 and 28 alone, specialists surveyed 602.8 hectares (1,490 acres) and neutralized 471 explosive devices, the administration reported on Oct. 29. Authorities said 74.5% of the territory designated for clearance on the region's right bank has now been cleared.

Russian general charged in absentia for missile strike on museum dedicated to 18th century Ukrainian philosopher
A Russian lieutenant general has been charged in absentia with ordering the strike on the Kharkiv Oblast museum dedicated to 18th-century philosopher Hryhorii Skovoroda, the Prosecutor General reported on Oct. 29.
On May 6, 2022, a Russian missile struck the museum, located in the village of Skovorodynivka, some 55 kilometers (about 35 miles) from the regional capital. The strike did not completely destroy the museum, but left it in serious disrepair.
According to the Prosecutor General, the Russian lieutenant general who ordered the attack is originally from the village of Chuhuiv in Kharkiv Oblast and commands Russia's 6th Guards Air and Air Defense Forces Army.
"The (lieutenant) general knew for certain that he was attacking not a military target but a monument of Ukrainian culture. Despite this, he gave the combat order to destroy it," the Prosecutor General wrote.
Skovoroda is considered one of the most influential philosophers in Ukrainian intellectual history. His written works are vital contributions to the Ukrainian Baroque and Enlightenment traditions. The building that housed the museum was once the estate where Skovoroda spent his final years and died in 1794.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's cultural heritage since the start of the full-scale war. As of September 2026, 2,161 cultural heritage sites and 2,665 cultural institutions in Ukraine had been damaged or destroyed, according to data collected by the Culture Ministry.

articles.title: Ukraine's Neptune Missiles Destroy 2 Russian Su-34 Bombers in Volgograd Region
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Neptunes successfully destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers, used by Moscow to launch unguided and guided aerial bombs (KABs), in Russia’s Volgograd region on Thursday, Oct. 29.
The Ukrainian Navy’s Neptune coastal missile system hit the aircraft, which can also carry missiles of various types, at the Marinovka airfield, near the settlement of Oktyabrsky. This was initially reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Several minutes later, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the report, noting that Ukraine had carried out two missile strikes during the day. In one of the strikes, a launcher for Russia’s Iskander ballistic missiles was hit as well.
The Su-34, a two-seat long-range strike derivative of the Su-27 fighter, was originally developed in the 1990s, but was only brought into service in 2014.
It is described as Russia’s main aircraft launching KABs on Ukrainian cities nationwide, capable of carrying up to 8 tons of munitions, with an estimated value of each jet at about $50 million.
Such bombs remain one of Russia’s most destructive weapons against Ukrainian cities near the front line. Earlier on Thursday, three KABs struck an apartment building in Izium, Kharkiv region, injuring at least 13 people.
Throughout the day, at least 20 people were killed and 109 wounded in Russian attacks on Ukraine nationwide, with several types of weapons used, including ballistic missiles and first-person-view (FPV) drones.
80% of Ukrainians Back Refinery Strikes Despite Risks of US Aid Cut
Second strike on Su-34 in two weeks
The Marinovka airfield, located about 400 kilometers (249 miles) from Ukraine, has previously been targeted by Ukrainian Defense Forces in 2025 as well, as it hosts a squadron of Su-34s.
Overnight Oct. 14-15, Ukraine struck six Russian Su-34 bombers with a Neptune missile strike, at another military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region. The attack targeted Borisoglebsk airfield and also destroyed equipment used to support flight operations
Originally designed to destroy warships, Neptune is a domestically developed Ukrainian Cruise missile. In April 2022, its ground-based system sank Russia’s shadow fleet vessel, the Moskva.
Since then, Ukraine has upgraded the missile for strikes on land targets deep inside Russia, with the new version capable of reaching targets up to 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) away.
Zelensky warns of fresh ballistic attacks
During the same remarks, Zelensky said Ukraine had obtained intelligence that Russia was preparing fresh ballistic missiles.
He called on partners to provide interceptor packages for Patriot air-defense systems, of which Ukraine is facing a critical shortage. “We are waiting for the relevant decisions,” Zelensky said.
The appeal follows similar warnings during his visit to the Netherlands on Wednesday, Oct. 28, where he described Patriot missiles as Ukraine’s most critical shortage, urging Washington not to delay deliveries under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism through which allies fund purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine.
Ahead of winter, Russia is increasingly relying on ballistic missiles to target Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water supplies.
Meanwhile, Kyiv has reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptors as early as Oct. 15, due to limited deliveries from allies.
For Ukraine the PAC-3 is among the very few weapons capable of deterring Russia’s ballistic missiles. Russian Iskander-M, for example, is a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead that is strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
“Another aspect of our anti-ballistic work is the interceptor packages, primarily for Patriots, that partners can provide to us,” Zelensky said on Wednesday.

articles.title: Poland hands Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets
articles.body:
- Poland will soon transfer two MiG-29 fighters to Ukraine in a new aid package worth about €50 million, Rzeczpospolita reported.
- One jet has reached the end of its service life and may be used for spare parts, while the other is still flying.
Poland will soon hand Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets as part of a new military aid package worth about €50 million (about $56 million), Polish daily Rzeczpospolita reported on Oct. 29, in a story quickly picked up by Ukrainian defense outlet Milarnyi.
Reserve Lt. Gen. Dariusz Łukowski, director of the Polish Defense Ministry’s Strategy and Defense Planning Department, confirmed the transfer to the newspaper and said the decision had been made, without giving a date beyond “in the near future.” Only one of the two jets is still flying. The other has reached the end of its service life, and Rzeczpospolita reported that Ukraine may use it as a source of spare parts.
The rest of the package is mostly munitions. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland will also send 155 mm and 152 mm artillery shells, 20 mm rounds for the six-barrel cannon fitted to F-16 fighters, which Ukrainian pilots use to shoot down Russian drones, and missiles for the Piorun shoulder-fired air defense system built by Polish manufacturer Mesko. Ukrainian defense officials had said in September that the Polish donation would be worth €50 million and would include air defense equipment. Poland’s Defense Ministry declined to detail the contents, saying only that the package draws on equipment being retired by the Polish armed forces or no longer needed.
The two aircraft are a small addition to a fleet Poland has been feeding since the early part of the war. Poland began openly handing over MiG-29s in March 2023, and by that May then-Defense Minister Mariusz Błaszczak said Ukraine had received 10 of them, Militarnyi reported. In total, Poland has given Ukraine 14 MiG-29s, Militarnyi said. Rzeczpospolita reported the same figure, adding that the jets were sent in 2022 and 2023 in varying technical condition and with little publicity.
A further transfer has been discussed for more than two years. In July 2024, Poland’s security agreement with Ukraine included a pledge to consider sending at least one more MiG-29 squadron, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Warsaw could not simply give up jets still flying air policing missions unless allies supplied replacements. At the time, the Polish Air Force still had 14 MiG-29s: 11 single-seat MiG-29As and three two-seat MiG-29UB trainers.
In late 2025, the two governments began talks on the last Polish MiG-29s. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the handover would benefit Poland because Warsaw would receive Ukrainian drone and missile technology in return. That exchange has not happened. As of mid-June 2026, Poland’s deputy defense minister said no aircraft from that batch had been delivered, and Rzeczpospolita reported the technology transfer stalled at the political level after Ukraine’s president named a military unit after heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a wartime nationalist force whose legacy is deeply contested in Poland.
Poland can spare the jets because their missions are moving to newer aircraft. The MiG-29 has kept a shrinking quick reaction alert role over the Baltic, and Rzeczpospolita reported that its tasks are now handled by Polish F-16s and the first 12 South Korean-built FA-50 light fighters, which reached full operational readiness in 2026.
For Ukraine, every additional airframe matters. The Ukrainian Air Force still relies heavily on the Soviet-designed MiG-29, which it has kept flying through deliveries from Poland, Slovakia and Bulgaria and through cannibalizing retired jets for parts, while losing aircraft to Russian strikes on airfields and in the air.
The new package also follows a separate Polish contribution of Patriot interceptors. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland has given Ukraine 10 PAC-3 MSE missiles in total, five earlier this year and five more through an international donation led by the United States with NATO. Kosiniak-Kamysz said in July that Poland’s donations to Ukraine since 2022 were worth about 16.45 billion zlotys, most of them delivered in 2022 and 2023, and the ministry later declassified the full list of transferred equipment.

articles.title: Russian Banderol Missile Kills Two 15-Year-Old Girls, Injures 15 in Chernihiv
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Banderol Missile Kills Two 15-Year-Old Girls, Injures 15 in Chernihiv
A Russian missile strike on central Chernihiv killed two 15-year-old girls and injured at least 15 people, including three children, on October 29, according to regional authorities.
Viacheslav Chaus, head of the Chernihiv regional military administration, identified the weapon as Russia's S8000 Banderol cruise missile in a statement published on the administration's official Telegram channel.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Russia killed two 15-year-old girls with its Banderol in central Chernihiv," Chaus wrote.
The missile struck during the day, when the city center was crowded with pedestrians. Eleven injured people were hospitalized, while medical personnel treated the other injured people at the scene. Businesses, residential buildings, and vehicles sustained extensive damage.
Emergency services continued working at the impact site as authorities assessed the destruction and casualties.
The S8000 Banderol is a Russian jet-powered cruise missile developed by the sanctioned defense manufacturer Kronstadt. Designed primarily for launch from Orion reconnaissance drones, the missile has a reported range of approximately 500 kilometers and carries a warhead weighing up to 150 kilograms.
According to Ukraine's Defense Intelligence, it can perform sharp maneuvers during flight while maintaining the trajectory of a conventional cruise missile.
Russia has been expanding production of Banderol missiles despite international sanctions targeting its defense industry. In August, Ukraine's military intelligence reported that Russian manufacturers were capable of producing up to 80 missiles per month. Intelligence officials also identified foreign-made electronics and components used in the weapon, including parts supplied through intermediaries despite restrictions on Russia's military-industrial sector.
The flow of Western technology into Russia's weapons factories has become a growing focus for Kyiv, which earlier in October appealed to employees of manufacturing, logistics, and trading companies for tips on illicit procurement networks.
To circumvent sanctions, Russian firms have reportedly relied on shell companies and complex supply routes through third countries to obtain microelectronics and dual-use goods.
The appeal came during a week when Russian strikes killed more than 100 Ukrainian civilians and injured over 400 others, including children, hitting residential buildings, passenger buses, shopping centers, and schools.

articles.title: North Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles amid rising tensions with South Korea
articles.body:
North Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles amid rising tensions with South Korea
North Korea fired around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, Seoul's defence ministry said. The North Korean capital Pyongyang has stepped up weapons tests in recent weeks despite South Korea's offer of military talks.
North Korea fired "around a dozen" short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, Seoul's defence ministry said, less than a week after South Korea proposed talks over a growing border row.
The launches follow a slew of recent weapons tests by Pyongyang, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology.
Read moreNorth Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said its military detected "around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea" – the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
The missiles flew about 250 kilometres, and "South Korea and the United States are conducting a detailed analysis of their exact specifications", Seoul's military said, adding it had stepped up surveillance of possible additional launches.
The Japan Coast Guard had earlier urged ships in the area to be vigilant.
Seoul's National Security Office meanwhile, said the launches violated UN Security Council resolutions, labelling them "serious acts that do nothing to help manage the current situation".
Thursday's missile flurry comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea planted the landmines over a year ago.
Seoul accused the North's capital Pyongyang of "a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement" and demanded an apology, something the North has mockingly dismissed.
'Show of force'
"This should be seen as a fairly high-level show of force," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, told AFP.
"North Korea is demonstrating that it has the capability to completely destroy major South Korean and US military facilities," he said.
Pyongyang was also sending a political message, Lim added, by "showing off its overwhelming military power and warning Seoul not to interfere with its efforts to fortify the border".
Last week, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, said the North would place loudspeakers on standby along the border "within days" and had put unspecified "new counter means" on alert.
Both countries have occasionally turned to loudspeakers blaring propaganda across their shared border and other psychological warfare methods.
South Korea days later proposed military talks with the North to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, but Pyongyang is yet to respond.
Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war, as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce, rather than a peace treaty.
The ratcheting tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to North Korea have raised concerns that Seoul – an ally of Washington – could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving Pyongyang.
In his most recent comments, Trump seemingly downplayed the possibility of a summit while insisting his relationship with Kim Jong-Un was "very good".
In October, North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested the two might meet this year.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Flash: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot missiles
articles.body:
Flash: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot missiles
According to a Ukrinform correspondent, this was stated during a briefing by Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a special advisor to the President.
“Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the world produces ‘Patriots’ to counter them. In other words, this balance looks very strange. If we add North Korean missiles to this, and the missiles produced by Iran, then we realize that global production of anti-ballistic missiles—such as the PAC-3, for example—needs to be increased. But there are currently problems and limitations, and while the Pentagon is trying to increase these production volumes, it’s difficult to do so,” Beskrestnov noted.
He noted that Ukraine could obtain licenses to manufacture anti-ballistic missiles, but the problem lies in the backlog for their components.
To address the shortage of anti-ballistic missiles, Ukraine is requesting that missiles be provided on loan, which it would later return once it begins domestic production; however, due to the unstable global situation, European partners are unwilling to agree to such a move. For its part, the U.S., which has a sufficient supply of PAC-3s, is very limited in how many it is willing to provide.
“These missiles are in the United States, and there’s a stockpile there—some say 3,000, others 4,000; there are 5,000 missiles in the U.S.—and to protect Kyiv, for example, where the ‘Patriot’ system is deployed, through the winter, we need about 4–5% of the U.S. stockpile. That’s a very small portion. And we’re asking the U.S.: ‘Give us this, because the Russians will destroy our infrastructure,’ but this requires a political decision. A decision from the U.S. government. They could give us these missiles—it wouldn’t affect their own defense, because, as I’ve already said, it’s literally 4 percent. But they won’t. We’re receiving a very small number, and we see what’s happening now. I actually believe this is our number one problem,” Beskrestnov noted.
According to the adviser, the situation on the front lines is currently stable, and Ukraine will be able to withstand the enemy even in the event of additional mobilization in Russia. At the same time, the biggest problem today is urban warfare and the enemy’s intention to completely destroy Ukraine’s economic potential.
“Even if they mobilize an additional 300,000 people, that solves nothing. We’ll simply produce more FPVs and field more crews to attack the Russians. We’re already facing the problem that our troops aren’t meeting their targets because there simply aren’t that many Russians to begin with. It sounds very strange, but it’s true. In other words, we understand that the war has changed,” the adviser noted.
According to him, the enemy is destroying infrastructure, bridges, and warehouses in order to cripple Ukraine’s economy.
Beskrestnov emphasized that the enemy is currently stockpiling missiles and “Shahed” drones to continue attacking critical infrastructure. Kyiv will be the primary target, as the capital is a symbolic city for the Russian occupiers.
“Kyiv is a symbolic place for our enemy. They understand that the government is here, and they understand that the international community is watching Kyiv. That is why they want to attack Kyiv specifically,” the adviser emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine currently needs an aid package consisting of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles from Europe and several other countries; subsequently, the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program will become operational, and contracts with Germany for the procurement of the relevant interceptors will take effect.

articles.title: Aid mission set to enter Ukraine's Oleshky as localised ceasefire holds for third day
articles.body:
Aid mission set to enter Ukraine's Oleshky as localised ceasefire holds for third day
A humanitarian aid mission is set to enter the Ukrainian town of Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said on Thuirsday, as a localised truce between Kyiv and Moscow, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, held for a third day. Some 2,000 residents in the Russian occupied city have been cut off from essential supplies amid reports that many are starving.
Humanitarian aid is poised to roll into the stricken city of Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said Thursday, as a localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared away landmines.
Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, but remain otherwise locked in the war that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion more than 4 ½ years ago. Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.
Elsewhere, a jet-powered Russian drone hit two passenger trains stopped at a station in Dnipro in central Ukraine on Thursday, killing at least 14 people and injuring 14 more, including a 40-year-old man whose legs were amputated, officials said.
Read moreAt least 13 killed in 'horrific' Russian drone strike at Ukraine train station
Also, a Russian cruise missile killed two 15-year-old girls in the northern city of Chernihiv, and three more civilians died when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in the central Ukraine city of Kremenchuk, authorities said. In all, 56 people were injured in the strikes, including 10 children.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said air defences downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv. Around half of the drones were heading to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.

Both sides thanked US first lady Melania Trump for what the White House said was her role in helping broker the temporary ceasefire so food and medical supplies can be delivered to some 2,000 desperate people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.
“The parties are fully adhering to the agreements, and no violations of the ceasefire have been reported,” Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday, adding that aid deliveries were due to begin the following day.
His Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the truce was holding and that Russian engineers are working on demining Oleshky's roads.
“Both sides are fully honoring their commitments, and no violations have been recorded,” she said. “This allows military personnel to continue clearing roads of mines and to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy.”
Local people will also be able to evacuate, either into Russia or Ukraine, officials say. The mechanics of how that might work are unclear.
Lantratova said she and her team were on their way to Oleshky for the aid delivery, adding that the operation was five months in the making.
Russian and Ukrainian representatives met in the Belarus city of Homel on Thursday to fly together to the Kherson region, Belarus state media reported.
A volunteer from Oleshky, Ksenia Arkhipova, told The Associated Press roughly 1,000 residents have told her they want to leave the city.
She said it was important that the Ukrainian delegation was present in Oleshky because many residents fear Russian authorities would identify individuals with pro-Ukrainian views or ties to Ukraine’s military.
In the nearby city of Kherson, growing numbers of people were out on the streets as the truce held.
Nataliia Myronenko, 42, had a steady stream of customers at her coffee kiosk since early Thursday.
“Now, during the quiet, we have people at lunchtime and in the evening, which we didn’t have under the attacks,” she said. “For a while, people would race down this street because they were afraid to stop.”
The pause has brought a sense of relief, she said. “It’s a breath of freedom, when you don’t look at the sky. You keep looking at your feet because of the mines, but you’re not afraid of dying. It’s so great,” she said.
“It’s such a privilege and a joy, but we understand it will end soon.”
Moscow and Kyiv are keen to curry favor with Washington ahead of possible three-way talks next month.
American military support is vital for Ukraine, but US President Donald Trump has waived sanctions on Russia and publicly chided Zelensky, indicating he is disengaging with Kyiv.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel are sailing to the United States, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov is expected to attend a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, starting Friday, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.
European leaders, on the other hand, have been trying to diplomatically isolate Russian President Vladimir Putin over Moscow’s invasion and what they call a campaign of sabotage across the continent.
Ukraine earlier this month reported sudden and unexpected limits on Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communications.
Putin said Russia has been in contact with the American tech titan to coordinate their orbiting activities because it is building its own equivalent of Starlink.
“Elon Musk is a genius. Truly, a real genius,” Putin said late Wednesday.
“We and our American partners value this relationship, and despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely together,” he added.

articles.title: India objects to US upgrade of Pakistani F-16s
articles.body:
India objects to US upgrade of Pakistani F-16s
India has raised objections to a $686 million US package to upgrade Pakistan’s F-16 fighter jets and extend their service life, Indian media have reported.
Washington has gone ahead with the upgrade even as India and the US continue to deepen defense cooperation under a ten-year partnership framework signed last year. India and Pakistan, both nuclear-armed, clashed briefly last year with drones and missiles following a terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 26 civilians.
Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, in his talks with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Wednesday, also raised the possibility of sensitive American military technology supplied to Pakistan reaching third countries, the Economic Times reported, citing officials familiar with the discussions. The two officials met on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus in Cebu, Philippines.
The proposed package, notified to the US Congress in December, is intended to modernize Pakistan’s aging F-16 fleet and extend their operational life through 2040.
It includes 92 Link-16 tactical communication systems, avionics upgrades, secure communications, navigation equipment, spare parts, and training, according to a US Defense Security Cooperation Agency notification published last month. The package does not involve the sale of new fighter jets, and the US agency said it would not alter the basic military balance in the region.
📹 'Our Strategies Are Battle-Tested': Rajnath Singh Cites Operation Sindoor At ADMM Defence Meet 💪💥 🇮🇳 DefMin cited the operation as proof of New Delhi's counter-terrorism methods being battle-tested. He also offered to share that experience with ASEAN partners through joint drills and intelligence sharing.
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 29, 2026
Washington has maintained that the upgrades would support cooperation with Pakistan in counterterrorism operations, improve coordination between the two countries’ air forces, and address aircraft safety concerns.
India has previously objected to American support for Pakistan’s F-16 fleet, including in 2022 when Washington approved a $450 million maintenance package. Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar also questioned Washington’s justification that the aircraft were needed for counterterrorism operations.
During Wednesday’s meeting, the two sides reviewed progress on military coordination, technology sharing, and defense production, according to India’s Defense Ministry. Its public statement did not mention the F-16 objection.
Singh called for a zero-tolerance approach toward nations supporting, training, or financing terrorist organizations, and Hegseth reaffirmed Washington’s support for India in combating cross-border terrorism.
Both ministers agreed to strengthen military exchanges, maritime security cooperation, and defense supply chains, with Singh describing the India-US partnership as a cornerstone of a free, open, and secure Indo-Pacific.

articles.title: North Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles into Sea of Japan: Seoul
articles.body:
North Korea fired "around a dozen" short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast on Thursday, Seoul's defence ministry said, less than a week after South Korea proposed talks over a growing border row.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said its military detected "around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea", the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
"Our military has stepped up surveillance and vigilance against possible additional launches," it added in its statement.
The Japan Coast Guard separately said that "an object that appears to be a ballistic missile launched from North Korea seems to have already fallen", urging ships to be vigilant.
North Korea has tested a slew of weapons recently, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology.
Thursday's flurry of missiles comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea planted the landmines over a year ago.
Seoul accused Pyongyang of "a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement" and called for the North to return to dialogue.
No response
Pyongyang has since ridiculed South Korean President Lee Jae-myung's overture, with Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of the North's leader, dubbing it "the climax of the farce".
Last week, South Korea proposed military talks with the North to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, but Pyongyang has yet to respond.
The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two countries.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war, as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
The ratcheting tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to North Korea have raised concerns that Seoul, an ally of Washington, could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving Pyongyang.
In his most recent comments, Trump seemingly downplayed the possibility of a summit while insisting his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un is "very good".
In October, North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested the two might meet this year.

articles.title: Fire breaks out at US nuclear weapons facility
articles.body:
Fire breaks out at US nuclear weapons facility
A fire broke out at a major nuclear research complex in South Carolina that supports the US nuclear weapons program, the Department of Energy has said.
The fire started at Savannah River National Laboratory, part of the Savannah River Site (SRS) near Aiken, on Wednesday evening and was subsequently extinguished, officials said.
“No contamination has been reported outside the affected facility,” the department said in a statement.
Emergency protocols were activated, with employees not involved in response efforts ordered to suspend operations and shelter in place as a precaution. The site was closed to incoming traffic, while nearby rail, river, and air traffic was restricted.
Officials lifted the emergency declaration at 9:45 PM, saying radiation surveys found no detectable contamination. Protective measures were lifted, and the site was cleared to resume normal operations on Thursday.
Local media reported that the fire broke out in a single room and involved an unfiltered, ground-level radiological release. One employee was reportedly hospitalized with minor injuries.
Established in the early 1950s during the Cold War, the SRS originally produced plutonium and tritium for US nuclear weapons. Although its production reactors have since been shut down, the complex continues to play a key role in maintaining the American nuclear arsenal.
The SRS processes and replenishes tritium, a radioactive isotope of hydrogen used to boost the explosive yield of nuclear warheads. It also manages nuclear materials, treats radioactive waste, and carries out environmental cleanup.
The US government is also developing a facility at the SRS to manufacture plutonium cores for nuclear warheads as part of efforts to modernize the country’s nuclear weapons stockpile.
The incident comes less than two weeks after a fire swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, killing four soldiers and injuring 39 others during a live-fire training exercise. According to the Canadian military, strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly, overtaking an area occupied by troops.
The Canadian Armed Forces said last week that 27 personnel remained hospitalized, while 12 were discharged. Military police have launched an independent investigation into the incident.

articles.title: Poland to transfer two more MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland to transfer two more MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine
That is according to Dariusz Lukowski, director of the Department of Strategy and Defense Planning at Poland's Ministry of National Defense, Ukrinform reports, citing Rzeczpospolita.
According to Lukowski, the decision has already been made, and the transfer will take place "in the near future."
However, the news outlet has learned that one of the aircraft has already reached the end of its service life and will likely be used for spare parts. The second fighter jet remains in service.
In addition to the aircraft, Poland will provide Ukraine with 155 mm and 152 mm artillery ammunition, 20×102 mm ammunition for the aircraft cannons of F-16 fighter jets, and Polish-made missiles for Piorun short-range man-portable air defense systems.
Poland's Ministry of National Defense confirmed that a new aid package was being prepared but did not disclose its full contents, citing the classified nature of the information. The ministry stressed that the scale of assistance would be determined with due regard for Poland's security and the resources available to its armed forces.
Rzeczpospolita notes that Poland has already transferred 14 MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine in 2022-2023.
The news oultet also reports that Poland is to provide Ukraine with five more PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles for Patriot systems as part of a U.S.-led international initiative in cooperation with NATO. Earlier this year, Warsaw had already transferred five such missiles.
In September, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said that Poland was preparing its largest military aid package for Ukraine and had no intention of reducing its support amid Russian attacks.

articles.title: Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
articles.body:
Ukraine destroys 2 Russian Su-34 bomber jets in Neptune missile strike on airfield, Navy says
Ukraine's Navy destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber jets in a strike against the Marinovka military airfield in Russia's Volgograd Oblast, using domestically produced Neptune missiles, the Navy reported on Oct. 29.
The aircraft were destroyed at the base of Russia's 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment near the settlement of Oktyabrsky, according to the Navy. The regiment belongs to the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of Russia's 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army. The Navy did not provide any visual confirmation of the strike. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
Later on Oct. 29, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the destruction of the two Su-34 jets, adding that Ukrainian forces had also hit a Russian Iskander missile launcher.
The Su-34 is one of Russia's main aircraft used to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, frontline settlements, and military positions. Strikes against these aircraft could weaken Russia's ability to carry out such attacks, while replacing the losses requires significant time and resources.
Russia had approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service as of Oct. 22, including the modernized Su-34M, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) reported on Oct. 29.
According to the agency, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed and another seven damaged since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Such losses are quite significant for the aggressor's aircraft fleet, whose restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, substantial financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation," HUR said.
The agency estimated that Russia can manufacture approximately 14 to 18 Su-34 aircraft annually, meaning the number of destroyed aircraft is equivalent to roughly 2.5–3 years of production.
Despite the losses, Russia continues to manufacture and modernize the aircraft to maintain its fleet and sustain aerial attacks against Ukraine.
The latest strike follows an Oct. 15 attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia's Voronezh Oblast that destroyed four Su-34M bomber-jets and damaged two more. The attack was also carried out using Neptune missiles.
The Ukrainian ground-launched Neptune cruise missile is best known for sinking Russia's Black Sea flagship, the Moskva, in 2022. Ukraine has since developed a longer-range version capable of striking targets up to 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) away.

articles.title: Merz stated that military cooperation between Russia and North Korea threatens Europe's security
articles.body:
Merz stated that military cooperation between Russia and North Korea threatens Europe's security
Kyiv • UNN
Merz stated that North Korean troops in the war against Ukraine threaten Europe's freedom. Germany and South Korea will deepen security cooperation.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that North Korea threatens "freedom throughout Europe" by sending its troops to fight on Russia’s side in the war against Ukraine. This was reported by DW, writes UNN.
Details
After a meeting in Seoul with South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, Merz emphasized that Russia supplies weapons to North Korea.
The chancellor said that such cooperation demonstrates how "the security of Korea affects the security of Europe. And the security of Europe also affects the security of Korea."
It is noted that North Korea has strengthened its military ties with Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pyongyang supplied Moscow with artillery ammunition and missiles. In addition, according to South Korean intelligence services, it sent about 15,000 troops to participate in combat operations on the side of Russian forces.
In return, Russia provides North Korea with financial support, military technologies, and security guarantees.
Before Merz’s arrival on Thursday, North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, the South Korean military reported.
At the beginning of his visit, Merz said he hoped for the future reunification of Korea. The peninsula has been divided along the 38th parallel since the end of the fighting in the Korean War in 1953.
Merz also agreed with Lee to deepen strategic and security cooperation between the two countries. This includes joint military exercises and the exchange of intelligence information.

articles.title: Pentagon watchdog refuses to investigate Starlink restrictions for Ukraine – AP
articles.body:
Pentagon watchdog refuses to investigate Starlink restrictions for Ukraine – AP
The Pentagon's oversight body, the Office of the Inspector General, has rejected a bipartisan request from US senators to investigate recent disruptions to the Starlink and Starshield services for Ukraine.
Source: Associated Press, citing sources, senators and the Pentagon's response
Details: The AP notes that this raises concerns among American lawmakers that the military and even the independent inspector general are unwilling to challenge the influence that SpaceX head Elon Musk has over the defence communications system.
A bipartisan group of senators asked the Pentagon's watchdog to conduct an investigation after Ukrainian officials reported in October that their connection speeds to the Starlink service and its military version Starshield, both created by Musk, had been restricted.
AP's report emphasises that these services are crucial for ensuring communications in Ukraine during the war, and Ukrainian officials stated that these restrictions hindered the interception of Russian jet attack drones.
In a response obtained by AP, the Pentagon watchdog informed the group of nine lawmakers – four Republicans and five Democrats – that the US Air Force would be better placed to answer their request regarding these concerns.
AP quotes a congressional aide familiar with the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity, who said this is viewed as a refusal by the inspector general to investigate Musk and Starlink, despite being fully capable to do so.
Quote from Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee: "It is concerning that the Inspector General has apparently decided not to investigate satellite communication disruptions that Ukraine relies on to protect its civilians."
Details: Shaheen added that "the Trump administration and SpaceX have provided conflicting accounts of what led to those disruptions" and that "there must be an independent accounting and review to determine responsibility and prevent this from happening in the future".
AP adds that the lack of answers raises questions about the extent of influence that Musk, an ally of President Donald Trump, has over this critical communications system.
The congressional aide told the publication that concerns on Capitol Hill regarding Musk's control over Starlink have existed for years and were one of the reasons for creating Starshield, the military version of the system.
When Mollie Halpern, a spokesperson for the Inspector General's Office, was asked about the decision regarding the investigation, she said the watchdog had "carefully considered the congressional request and determined that the matters raised were best addressed by the Department", referring to the Pentagon.
Halpern later added that if new information arises, the Pentagon may revisit its decision.
The Pentagon referred a request for comment to the Inspector General's Office, while the Air Force did not immediately respond to messages requesting comment. Both had previously declined to answer questions regarding the restriction of Ukraine's access to satellite internet.
Background:
- Nine lawmakers asked the Pentagon inspector general to investigate whether any Pentagon or other US government officials had "directed, authorised, approved or had advance knowledge of changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements, warning capabilities, or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine".
- On 24 October, SpaceX owner Elon Musk commented on restrictions on access to Starlink, claiming that the Ukrainian military had violated the terms of use for this type of communications system. He also said that if Starlink were switched off, "the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".
- On 21 October, after information about the speed reduction became public, Musk wrote: "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
- Meanwhile, according to The Wall Street Journal, Musk ordered a speed reduction for the military version of Starlink for Ukraine, which rendered a portion of Ukrainian strike drones and interceptor drones practically unusable.
- On 22 October, the WSJ learned that US President Donald Trump had allegedly called Elon Musk and asked him to lift the restrictions on Starshield in Ukraine.
- On 19 October, Zelenskyy said that Starlink and Starshield equipment had stopped working at speeds of 130-161 km/h in various sectors of the front line, disrupting logistics and limiting Ukraine's use of drones.
- Zelenskyy believes that publicity surrounding the connection restrictions has helped to restore the Starlink system's operation to the required speed.

articles.title: 'Horrific' Russian drone strike kills 13 at Ukraine train station: Kyiv

At least 13 killed in 'horrific' Russian drone strike at Ukraine train station
At least 13 people were killed when a Russian drone struck a busy railway station in Ukraine's Dnipro on Thursday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, describing the attack as "horrific" and urging Kyiv's allies not to ease sanctions on Moscow.
A Russian drone slammed into a busy platform at a railway station in Ukraine's Dnipro on Thursday killing at least 13 people in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called a "horrific" attack that demands a response from Kyiv's allies.
The strike on the city located in the east of the country came as Ukraine and Russia strive to uphold a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky – which has been subject to Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages.

The truce was holding into its third day, both countries said, with the Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets announcing that he had "set out with the Ukrainian delegation towards Oleshky" through Belarus and Russia.

Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three jet-powered drones in a daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station.
The head of Ukraine Railways, Oleksandr Pertsovsky, said an elevated threat level had been announced.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform," he said on Facebook.
In the aftermath of the attack, Zelensky refreshed his criticism of a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to ease some sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel onto global markets.
"How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating," he asked.
At least five others were killed across Ukraine in separate Russian attacks, according to local officials.
Two teenagers killed
A strike on the city centre of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded more than a dozen, the head of the city's military administration, Dmytro Bryzhynsky, said.
A drone also slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing two and wounding several – including a six-year-old – the local governor said.
Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.

Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.
Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.
Ukraine and its allies say ceding ground to Moscow would be tantamount to a capitulation and leave Kyiv vulnerable to future Russian attacks.

articles.title: Turkey and Israel's growing rivalry in the Horn of Africa
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey and Israel's growing rivalry in the Horn of Africa
The Horn of Africa is where strategic maritime corridors, fragile states, and regional ambitions converge - and it is emerging as a new front in Middle Eastern geopolitical competition.
Israel’s 26 December 2025 recognition of Somaliland’s independence added new dimensions to these tensions, intersecting with Turkey’s expanding military, economic, and diplomatic footprint in Somalia and broader partnerships across the Horn of Africa.
From Turkey’s perspective, Israel’s Somaliland move and its broader regional engagement challenge Ankara’s strategic interests. Tel Aviv, for its part, views Somaliland as a potential gateway to projecting influence near Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen and along one of the world’s most important maritime corridors.
Somaliland’s longstanding quest for international recognition risks becoming further entangled in the rivalries of Middle Eastern powers, transforming a local sovereignty dispute into a wider contest over the future of Red Sea security.
As Turkey and Israel deepen their engagement, and other external actors pursue their own agendas, the Horn of Africa might end up an increasingly crowded arena of geopolitical competition. The implications for regional stability could be serious.
Israel's Somaliland gambit and the rivalry with Turkey
Situated alongside busy maritime routes, the Horn of Africa links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, occupying a position of much geostrategic importance.
Egypt, Iran, Israel, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) increasingly view the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the surrounding territories as a single security environment. Instability in one part of this interconnected region can disrupt commercial shipping, threaten energy security, and intensify rivalries among states far beyond its shores.
Israel’s decision to recognise Somaliland’s independence and to invest in deeper ties with the self-declared breakaway republic is very much about securing a strong position in a territory situated in close proximity to Yemen.
This land can provide Tel Aviv with the means to closely monitor Houthi activity, improve intelligence collection, and strengthen surveillance of maritime routes that have become increasingly vulnerable to disruption.
“Israel’s interest in the Horn of Africa is not new but has sped up amid regional shake-up in the aftermath of [7 October 2023],” Dr Burcu Ozcelik, Senior Research Fellow for Middle East Security at the London-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab.
“Israel sees Somaliland mainly through a defence cooperation lens, and as a possible staging ground for future offensive military activity against the Houthis. The strategic value of access near Yemen for Israel spans intelligence, surveillance, and potentially military operations,” she added.
Ankara and Tel Aviv’s rivalry and maritime security interests are “mutually reinforcing” motivations, argued Cameron Hudson, an independent analyst with expertise on African peace, security, and governance, who previously worked on Africa at the Central Intelligence Agency, State Department, and the US National Security Council.
“They are two sides of the same coin and cannot be disaggregated,” he told The New Arab.
However, Omar S. Mahmood, a Senior Analyst for Somalia and the Horn of Africa at International Crisis Group, offers a more qualified interpretation. He suggests that the immediate motivation for Tel Aviv is mostly related to security, while competition with Ankara is a secondary consequence, not necessarily the driving force.
“I don’t think Israel’s relationship with Somaliland is driven by a broader rivalry with Turkey per se. But there are local ramifications as Somaliland itself is seeking external allies as it is uncomfortable with growing Turkish military support to Somalia, viewing it as a potential future threat,” explained Mahmood in an interview with The New Arab.
“So, in this sense the middle powers can get drawn into supporting opposite sides in local rivalries, even if that was not the primary factor driving their engagement in the first place,” he added.
Turkey's foothold in Somalia
Turkey’s presence in Somalia is a product of many years of sustained investment and political commitment.
In 2011, Somalia faced a devastating famine which claimed approximately 250,000 lives (half of them children) amid an unprecedented humanitarian crisis. At that time, Mogadishu did not have many reliable partners around the world.
That was when Ankara’s engagement with the country gained momentum, beginning with humanitarian assistance and reconstruction before developing into a much wider relationship across multiple domains, from investment to military training and security cooperation to state-building.
Central to Turkey’s military partnership with Somalia has been its TURKSOM facility in Mogadishu. This training establishment has been at the heart of Turkish efforts to help build up the Somali government’s ability to fight al-Shabaab.
Ankara and Mogadishu signed a 10-year defence agreement in 2024, extending their cooperation into naval development and the protection of Somalia's coastline, alongside growing Turkish interests in maritime security and offshore oil and gas exploration, underscoring Turkey’s stakes in Somalia achieving greater stability.
Bilateral ties also strengthened when Somalia sought international support following Ethiopia's agreement with Somaliland concerning access to the sea in exchange for recognition - a deal which infuriated officials in Mogadishu.
Ankara subsequently helped mediate between Somalia and Ethiopia, illustrating how Turkey’s influence has gone beyond military and economic cooperation and entailed effective regional diplomacy.
In late 2025, Turkey joined many other countries around the world in strongly denouncing Israel’s recognition of Somaliland. Ankara feared that recognition of the breakaway republic gravely threatened Somalia’s territorial dignity.
Turkey also has concerns about the potential creation of openings for external actors to establish a presence for themselves in territories situated near maritime routes where Ankara has vested interests.
Rather than reacting with an immediate escalation of its military presence, Ankara seems to find its most effective response to be based on reinforcing its relationships and institutions that serve to underpin Turkish influence in Somalia. This measured approach appears to be aimed at protecting the investments which Turkey has made in the country without setting Ankara up for any overt confrontation with the Israelis in Somalia.
However, Ankara’s efforts to preserve its position in Somalia could have unintended consequences. Somaliland may interpret deeper Turkish-Somali security cooperation as a threat to its political ambitions, prompting Hargeisa to seek stronger external backing and, in the process, potentially deepening regional tensions.
The Emirati factor
No analysis of Turkish-Israeli competition in the Horn of Africa is complete without taking stock of the UAE’s role. Abu Dhabi’s support for Somaliland, even if short of formal recognition, places the UAE broadly on the same side of this sovereign dispute as Tel Aviv.
The UAE has vast strategic and commercial interests across the Red Sea, giving Abu Dhabi high stakes in the Horn of Africa’s evolving security order, while its normalised relationship with Israel continues to be an important feature of the Middle East’s geopolitical landscape more than six years after the Abraham Accords’ signing.
On the other side, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, and other regional actors have expressed support for Somalia’s territorial integrity, a position that connects their interests in the Horn of Africa to their wider security cooperation in the Middle East.
Hudson sees the UAE and Israel as a “powerful and mutually reinforcing duo in the Red Sea” which are both willing to challenge established power structures and intervene in disputes in the Horn of Africa to further their national interests at the region’s expense.
“They are happy to pick winners and losers, unsettle established power dynamics, and actively intervene in regional politics and conflicts in ways that benefit them even if that means unsettling regional dynamics,” he told The New Arab.
Hudson contrasts this with “Turkish or Saudi efforts to stabilise and reinforce established power dynamics as a way of limiting destabilising outside influences.”
Clearly, Abu Dhabi’s role is important not only due to Emirati ambitions but also because external backing can make local leaders less willing to compromise by reducing the perceived costs associated with confrontation.
The local stakes of a wider geopolitical contest
Despite the growing involvement of Middle Eastern states in the Horn of Africa, and the risks of this region becoming more of an arena for external competition, it is necessary to note that Somalia and Somaliland are not passive actors victimised by a giant game of geopolitical chess.
Both have agency and are actively seeking non-African partners to strengthen their positions and advance their political objectives.
For the government in Mogadishu, Turkey's military, economic, and diplomatic support is critical to strengthening state institutions, improving security, and protecting Somalia’s territorial integrity.
Meanwhile, Somaliland has long sought international recognition and has strong incentives to cultivate relationships with countries such as Israel and the UAE, which might advance that goal or at least provide greater protection against perceived threats.
In this sense, “you have a layer of local rivalries that now intersect with regional rivalries, creating a potentially dangerous situation,” explained Mahmood, who emphasised that this permits “Horn of Africa actors to take on more maximalist, aggressive and less compromising positions, knowing that [they] have…external support to fall back on.”
Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, Israel, and maritime targets have done much to help explain why regional powers see the Horn of Africa as increasingly important to their foreign policy calculations.
As Houthi-Saudi hostilities escalate, Riyadh is focused on growing stronger security partnerships with regional actors, while governments in the Horn of Africa are likely to view closer cooperation with the Kingdom as a way to secure higher levels of assistance and bolster their own military capabilities. Meanwhile, the conflict in Sudan adds new layers of complication as it draws regional actors into overlapping security and political calculations.
Yet a greater military presence does not necessarily translate into greater stability. While competing powers expand their security footholds with the aim of countering one another, mistrust can deepen, territorial disputes can intensify, and local actors will probably pursue greater support from external powers.
Therefore, the Horn of Africa is increasingly likely to become exposed to conflicts in and around the Red Sea even if not directly involved in their initial escalation. Within this context, heightened insecurity means that further militarisation of the Red Sea risks undermining, rather than enhancing, security.
An evolving security arrangement around the Red Sea
On 7 August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement - a trilateral alliance which is defensive in nature and aimed at containing the chaotic instability unleashed by the war centred on Iran.
This security configuration has potentially significant implications for the balance of power around the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. It was hardly surprising that the leadership in Mogadishu hailed the pact in the immediate aftermath of its announcement, especially given Somalia’s close ties with the three signatories and shared threat perceptions of Israeli aggression.
For Somalia, the pact’s significance extends beyond its endorsement and raises important questions about regional realignments and Ankara’s position in the Horn of Africa within the wider context of an emerging security architecture.
Escalating Houthi-Saudi hostilities prompt a broader recalibration of regional security alignments, bringing Turkey and Pakistan closer to Saudi Arabia through the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. For Ankara, this partnership offers an opportunity to connect its longstanding presence in Somalia with a wider strategic role in Gulf and Red Sea security.
Dr Ozcelik told The New Arab that the hostilities have “crossed red lines that were deemed unthinkable not long ago,” setting in motion a realignment among Riyadh’s allies. Ankara’s growing institutional engagement with the Kingdom therefore extends beyond diplomatic rhetoric, highlighting a more formal commitment to regional defence and security cooperation.
There are implications of this emerging Turkish-Saudi alignment for the rivalry between Ankara and Tel Aviv. As Dr Ozcelik stressed, Ankara is “institutionalising its partnership with Saudi Arabia beyond rhetoric and through defence commitments, minilateralism, and regional diplomacy.”
This closer Turkish-Saudi relationship will not escape Israeli strategists’ attention, particularly as Ankara expands its regional security role while Riyadh remains firm in its support for Palestinian statehood.
In Dr Ozcelik’s assessment, these parallel developments risk “fuelling a greater gulf between Israel and Turkey,” further complicating an already tense relationship that has significantly deteriorated since 7 October 2023.
While commentators sometimes toss Somalia around as a possible Mecca Joint Defence Agreement candidate, Hudson considers formal Somalia membership in the pact unlikely in the near term. He noted that Somalia remains a recipient of security assistance rather than a country capable of contributing meaningfully to a mutual defence arrangement.
“Given the high level of instability still emanating from Somalia, external countries would be foolish at this point to enter into a mutual security agreement with them now. Somalia can’t provide for its own security, let alone contribute to the security of others,” Hudson told The New Arab.
Similarly, Mahmood does not expect Somalia to formally join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. But he does think Mogadishu is likely to deepen security relations with the pact’s three signatories, noting that this is a development already underway. “Somalia prefers to align with this bloc of countries and sees them as a future source of support as it continues to build up its military capabilities,” he observed.
The risks of an expanding geopolitical contest
The internationalisation of the Horn of Africa’s political disputes and security crises entered a new chapter after Israel became the first UN member-state to officially recognise Somaliland ten months ago.
What started as a dispute over Somaliland’s recognition and Somalia’s territorial integrity has transformed into a larger contest over maritime security, military access, and regional influence.
A dangerous risk is an exacerbating security dilemma in which competing alliances deepen mistrust, undermine compromise, and expose the Horn of Africa to conflicts originating elsewhere.
Preventing further escalation will require Middle Eastern powers and their regional partners to exercise restraint while recognising that lasting stability depends on addressing the disputes that drive Somalia and Somaliland to seek competing external allies.

articles.title: Six lanes and metro line under fire: Kyiv prepares about $22 million for backup river crossings after Russian strike on Southern Bridge
articles.body:
The Ukrainian government has instructed Kyiv to establish alternative routes after Russian attacks stopped traffic on one of the capital’s main bridges. The city authorities will bear the cost of the new crossings, with Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko saying the city needs an additional $22 million.
This year, Russia has launched tactics to spread panic among civilians and trigger more people to leave the country. In the latest attack, several Russia's ballistic missiles struck the Southern Bridge, used for vehicle and metro traffic, breaking a huge hole and paralyzing all the pathes. The bridge was closed. Now, there is a fear that more bridges can be targeted this way, dividing Kyiv in two parts.
The situation is urgent, as Ukrainian Transport Minister Mykola Kalashnyk says about 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro in Kyiv every day.
What is Kyiv’s response to the winter terror?
According to Klitschko, Kyiv convened the capital’s Defense Council on 28 October to find an answer to this difficult question.
The agenda included implementing a project to build combined water crossings over the Dnipro River and access roads to them.
“The military command will determine the locations, with approval to be granted, among others, by the Kyiv City Military Administration,” Klitschko said.
Under the government’s recommendations, the Kyiv city authorities must find $22 million for the project.
Klitschko had previously faced heavy criticism after it emerged that the city lacked sufficient shelters and last winter exposed serious shortcomings in preparing infrastructure for Russian attacks. These included a lack of alternative energy supply routes, poorly distributed energy, burst heating pipes that flooded apartments, and the inability of people with disabilities to reach shelters without elevators.
The mayor himself said the problems stemmed from the central government withholding funding, which had stalled numerous energy resilience projects and delayed their implementation.
The latest announcement also indicates that Kyiv has once again taken on the financial burden itself.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has been working with Japan on backup crossings. Tokyo has already delivered 720 meters of prefabricated bridge structures to Ukraine. The two sides are currently exploring how this equipment could be used to establish alternative crossings.
Step two: strengthening existing infrastructure
Another option is to reinforce existing bridges. City specialists are developing additional technical solutions to protect bridges across the Dnipro River, Klitschko said in his statement on 27 October, adding that proposals from the military had also been heard.
The issue of installing mobile shelters was also raised on the same day, the mayor of Kyiv said in a separate statement on his Telegram channel on 27 October. Despite intensifying Russian attacks and about, as Radio Svoboda reported in its article on 30 September, $11 million set aside in 2025, Kyiv still has only a handful of mobile shelters: LB reported in December 2025 that district tenders failed. Donors paid for the first one at a bus stop, the Kyiv City State Administration said on 15 October.
Klitschko raised the issue of shelters again after a court on 12 October ruled that local authorities must urgently install mobile shelters in public areas, including near public transport stops, parks, and squares, according to Kyiv’s Prosecutor’s Office.
Russia hits the Southern Bridge again
On 2 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times that Russian ruler Vladimir Putin had ordered the lifting of previous restrictions on airstrikes. Among new targets, according to him, were bridges, data centers, internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, and universities.
The night of 26–27 October showed what that looks like. Russia launched ballistic missile attacks in a few waves, and the second of them hit the Southern Bridge and the metro infrastructure on it, Klitschko said. The structure carries six lanes of road traffic and two metro tracks.
Zelenskyy put the night’s total at 16 ballistic missiles and blamed delays in deliveries of Patriot and NASAMS interceptors: “Every such delay is a new Russian hit on one target or another.”
