articles.title: Israel eyes Covenant’s low-cost Anthem cruise missile
articles.body:
- Israeli Defense Ministry Director General Amir Baram visited Covenant, maker of the Anthem cruise missile, focusing on munitions independence and production capacity.
- Baram said the ministry backs both defense-tech startups and established industries, calling defense exports a critical growth engine.
Israel’s Defense Ministry Director General, retired Maj. Gen. Amir Baram, has visited Covenant, the startup behind the Anthem low-cost cruise missile, in a tour the ministry said focused on strengthening Israel’s munitions independence, expanding its production base and preserving the country’s qualitative and technological edge in the years ahead.
The ministry said on social media on Oct. 29 that the stop was part of a series of visits by Baram to leading defense companies under its strategy to strengthen Israel’s defense-tech ecosystem, in which the ministry acts as the integrating body between the Israel Defense Forces and the defense industry. It did not announce an order or agreement with Covenant.
“The Ministry’s policy is to encourage and strengthen both defense-tech companies and new startups, as well as the established industries. This balance is essential for fostering healthy competition, driving innovation and out-of-the-box thinking, maintaining our qualitative edge, and developing ‘the next surprises,'” said Baram.
“We must look ahead to an intense security decade and adapt our plans to both global changes and the evolution of the battlefield. Defense exports are a critical growth engine and an enabling tool, not only for strengthening the economy, but also for building the IDF’s force and delivering a critical mass of advanced systems to the warfighters on the front lines,” he said.
Covenant, founded in 2024 by Michael Kaufman and Ofir Dayan, kept its work secret until Sept. 9, when it unveiled Anthem and disclosed more than $250 million raised across three rounds led by Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, Lux, 8VC, Aleph and Lightspeed, Tectonic reported. The company is headquartered in Washington and runs a research, development and production site in Israel alongside factories in Texas and Germany.
Anthem is a ground-launched cruise missile that uses a solid rocket motor to get airborne and a jet engine burning heavy fuel for the cruise phase, and Covenant says it was designed from the start to be built in the thousands at a fraction of the cost of older systems such as the Tomahawk. The company has not disclosed the missile’s price, range or exact payload. Since its first flight in August 2025, Anthem has completed more than 200 test flights, including several with U.S. forces in the United States and abroad, though it has not been used in combat.
Covenant says it has booked about $150 million in orders covering qualification, development and production, along with a roughly $70 million cost-sharing agreement with the U.S. Navy’s Rapid Capabilities Office to develop a maritime version of the missile. Earlier this month, Denmark said it would buy ground-launched Anthem missiles to be built in Leipzig, Germany, where Covenant’s production line is due to open in 2027, while Germany’s Defense Ministry is also in talks with the company as it evaluates low-cost cruise missiles.
Baram’s push for munitions independence, meaning Israel can build critical weapons and components without relying on foreign supply chains, has taken him to several manufacturers this year, including loitering munition maker Uvision in July. In August he met the heads of about 20 defense-tech and startup companies, and the ministry said then that the number of defense-tech firms under its oversight had grown to 322 since the start of the war, with its orders from them reaching about $330 million, roughly double the same period a year earlier.

articles.title: Financial Times refuses to correct Putin call ‘disinformation’ – media
articles.body:
Financial Times refuses to correct Putin call ‘disinformation’ – media
The Financial Times has refused to correct an anonymously sourced article about a recent phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and the leaders of Norway and Finland, despite objections from both Nordic governments.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb spoke with Putin earlier this week, drawing criticism from some of Europe’s more Russia-hawkish politicians. Store has since demanded the FT retracts its reporting on teh conversation.
The British newspaper claimed that Putin spent significant time “lecturing” the Nordic leaders on “medieval Slavic history” and its relevance to the Ukraine conflict. Citing three anonymous sources described only as “familiar with the conversation,” the FT portrayed the Russian president as “fixated” on history.
Store’s government told Norwegian daily Verdens Gang (VG) that the characterization was inaccurate and that Finland had contacted the FT on behalf of both countries to challenge its account. Finnish media also covered the joint refutation, with the newspaper Helsingin Sanomat citing its own sources to dispute the British paper’s description of the call.
Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov said later in the day that the FT article is “some invented information, or rather disinformation” and that the Nordic leaders were correct to call out the publication.
The FT, however, rejected the request, telling VG that it stood by its reporting.
Its article, published on Tuesday, was written by three journalists.
One of them, American national Christopher Miller, previously worked for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, a US government-funded international broadcaster originally established with covert CIA funding to conduct anti-communist propaganda operations during the Cold War. Miller went to Ukraine in 2010 as a volunteer with the US Peace Corps.
His co-authors, Max Seddon and Henry Foy, head the FT’s bureaus in Moscow and Brussels, respectively.
Last week, the newspaper published a lengthy article by Seddon titled “The Putin whisperers,” recounting a dramatic but difficult-to-verify story of American and German nationals attempting to avert a “nuclear Armageddon” through backchannel diplomacy with Moscow.
Foy, notoriously broke a story in 2025 alleging that a plane carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had experienced suspected Russian GPS jamming. The FT journalist was himself aboard the aircraft when it landed in Bulgaria.
Key elements of the story were challenged almost immediately by flight-tracking service Flightradar24. Bulgarian authorities subsequently debunked the core claims relayed by FT.
Despite the discrepancies, the FT insisted it stood by its reporting. Foy did not respond to requests for comment from fellow journalists who questioned the account.

articles.title: How Europe Is Defying Trump by Rallying Around the ICC
articles.body:
As the Trump Administration forges ahead with its campaign to dismantle the International Criminal Court (ICC) “brick by brick,” Europe is publicly showing a steady stream of support for the institution.
The E.U. last week awarded the court and its officials the Sakharov human rights prize, commending “the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice.” The prestigious recognition came after former ICC judge Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay on Oct. 9 was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize—an honor long coveted by President Donald Trump. Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, acknowledged the award was intended to send a “message to those who are attacking, undermin[ing]... the international rules-based system.” Hours after Pillay’s win, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sweeping new sanctions against the ICC. While previous U.S. sanctions had targeted the institution's prosecutors and judges, the new measures were aimed at “cutting off [the court’s] resources” by severing U.S. transactions with the court.
Experts warn that the sanctions could have “extremely disruptive” implications for the court, especially in regards to financial support for case work, travel to the U.S. for judges, and the core functions of the institution itself. “Leaving the political dimension to one side, the rule of law and the just resolution of disputes depends, to a large extent, on the body in question having all available evidence,” says Nabil Khabirpour, an affiliated lecturer in E.U. law and jurisprudence at Cambridge University. “Organizations that are involved in working with witnesses, both on the ground and within the legal infrastructure, are likely to be affected.”
The latest sanctions, which were announced with a six-month initial grace period, are part of a broader push by the Trump Administration to dismantle the institution it accuses of unfairly targeting the U.S. and Israel. The Trump Administration has staunchly criticized the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and former investigations into the actions of American soldiers in Afghanistan. The ICC is recognized as the world’s highest criminal court. It draws its jurisdiction from the Rome Statute, a treaty that went into effect in 2002 and is ratified by 125 countries. Neither the U.S. nor Israel is a state party to the Rome Statute, and therefore they do not recognize the jurisdiction of the court.
Trump has long complained that the ICC oversteps its authority and should not claim jurisdiction over U.S. citizens. He amplified his campaign against the organization at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, taking time out of his 45-minute speech to publicly call on “all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution, immediately.” He said the U.S. is “opposed to the out-of-control institution known as the ICC” and “will never allow U.S. service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us.”
His call to action was swiftly rejected by European leaders.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, shortly after the speech, said: "We will, of course, not be doing that." In an interview with Germany's Deutschlandfunk radio station, he described the court as "an important institution” and said the issue is "one of the areas where we do indeed have to acknowledge a regrettable difference in policy from the U.S. Administration."
Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten also defended the ICC, asking how can anyone “possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?”
“I believe there can be only one response,” he continued, in his own U.N. address. “To say: 'hands off' the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order.” The remarks drew loud applause from attending delegates.
Similarly, European Council president Antonio Costa stressed that the E.U. stands “firmly behind” the ICC and argued it’s “unacceptable to threaten or attack the International Criminal Court, its officials, and its staff.”
The European Union as an organization has since strongly criticized the U.S. sanctions against the ICC. In a speech on Oct. 20, E.U. policy chief Kaja Kallas said the most recent “misguided” measures were “against” European interests.
“The U.S. has already adopted individual sanctions, including against nine judges and the chief prosecutor of the ICC. The latest U.S. announcement [on Oct. 9] to impose institutional sanctions puts the entire court at risk,” she argued, adding that Brussels will use the next six months "to open dialogue and look for solutions.”
European lawmakers call for “concrete” action against U.S. sanctions
The European Commission’s choice to take time to consider how to counter the U.S. sanctions has fallen short of what many European lawmakers have called for.
Several leading MEPs, including Germany's David McAllister, chair of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, and France's Mounir Satouri, chair of the Subcommittee on Human Rights, issued a public statement on Oct. 9 calling for the Commission to activate a legislative shield referred to as the “blocking statute,” which would essentially prevent E.U. firms from complying with U.S. sanctions.
“The European Union must now demonstrate unwavering solidarity with the ICC and its personnel—not only with words, but also with concrete acts,” the leading Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) said in a joint statement. “The European Commission must immediately trigger the E.U. blocking statute, shielding the court and European actors from the extraterritorial reach of these sanctions. Europe must stand firm in defence of international law and the rule of law."
This request was bolstered as 58 MEPs reportedly sent a letter to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen for the Commission to activate the measure.
According to the Commission, the purpose of the European Union’s blocking statute is to “protect E.U. operators from the extra-territorial application of third country laws.” The blocking statute came into force in 1996 in direct response to the U.S. sanctions against Cuba. The aim of the measure was to protect economic operators within the E.U. from the effects of such extraterritorial sanctions, according to the Norton Rose Fulbright law firm. As such, the blocking statute shields European economic operators from the application of the U.S. legislation and sanctions specified in the Annex to the E.U. blocking statute. More recently, the E.U.'s updated blocking statute entered into force in response to U.S. sanctions on Iran after the U.S. withdrew from the nuclear agreement in 2018.
Kallas has expressed an openness to the measure, but also advised caution when delivering her statement on European support for the ICC. “We should keep all options on the table. If we use the blocking statute, we have one shot and we should do it well. So, it should be well prepared," Kallas said, urging companies “not to over comply” with the sanctions, as they are not yet in effect.
ICC prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told the Guardian last week that some ICC staff are already facing "banking difficulties," despite the grace period before the sanctions come into effect. Khan said the banks were “over complying” to minimize risk amid uncertainty over the scope of the measures. She said the court's work has not been hindered.
TIME has reached out to the ICC for comment.
If the E.U. were to activate the blocking statute, it would be a “very important gesture” that could show the Trump Administration how “Europe is serious about protecting the court and that it is prepared to take real steps in that direction,” says Sergey Vasiliev, a professor of international law at Open University Netherlands. But he warns that some may view it as a “very extreme or radical measure, that could perhaps anger the Trump Administration even more” at a time where U.S.-Europe relations are already strained.
Meanwhile, some ICC officials have suggested alternative measures in an effort to mitigate the expected impact of the U.S. sanctions. Osvaldo Zavala Giler, the court's registrar, told Politico that “comfort letters” could be sent out, reassuring firms that they needn’t comply with the U.S. measures.
But Vasiliev argues that this “will not necessarily solve the problem, because businesses are expecting clear assurances of protection… the only such assurance can be provided by the actual triggering of the blocking statute.”
Could the ICC row further escalate U.S.-Europe tensions?
Relations between Europe and the U.S. have been under increasing strain since Trump returned to office in January 2025.
Trump has introduced various waves of tariffs on international trading partners, and has threatened further levies on the E.U. and member states in response to divisive issues.
When Trump’s pursuit of acquiring Greenland as a U.S. territory reached a critical point in January, Trump threatened to tariff European countries that opposed his campaign—a move that earned him strong rebuke from within his own party.
Last month, when von der Leyen invited Canada to work toward becoming the European Union’s first “associate member,” in what she described as an “urgent” reimagining of partnerships, Trump again threatened economic pressure. He called the proposal “laughable” and threatened to “put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things” if such an idea were to go ahead.
The Trump Administration has also clashed with its NATO allies. Earlier this year, Trump refused to rule out leaving the alliance over Greenland disputes, and since the start of the Iran war, the President has hit out at NATO countries for refusing to get actively involved in the conflict.
Should Brussels and Washington continue to clash on the ICC sanctions, “this could risk accelerating certain destabilizations, such as what we've seen with the trade wars,” says Khabirpour. International organizations will ultimately stand to suffer if the two remain at odds, he adds.

articles.title: Army standing up a Deep Recce Strike Brigade
articles.body:
The Army has approved and is implementing a Deep Recce Strike Brigade to pull intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and precision strike together at corps level, including what the department calls novel one-way effectors, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Stuart Anderson, the Conservative member for South Shropshire, asked what progress had been made on accelerating the development and deployment of the new Recce-Strike approach set out on page 111 of the Strategic Defence Review.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Army has approved and is implementing a Deep Recce Strike Brigade to provide Corps-level (HQ ARRC) integration of intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and precision strike capabilities, including novel one-way effectors. The 5th Generation Land Force programme will increase human-machine teaming, autonomy and decision advantage, further accelerating recce-strike capability across the force.”
A one-way effector is a munition that does not come back, in practice a loitering munition or an attack drone, and the phrase has become the department’s preferred term for a class of weapon that Ukraine has turned into the dominant means of killing vehicles and artillery well behind the line of contact.
The headquarters named is the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks in Gloucester, a NATO corps headquarters Britain provides and commands. The brigade’s output therefore arrives at the level where a corps commander shapes a battle, above divisional and brigade level.
The Strategic Defence Review published in June 2025 set out recce-strike as the organising idea for the future Army, describing a mix of sensors, long-range fires and autonomous systems connected by a digital targeting network. The Defence Investment Plan put £1.8 billion into that targeting web, and the Army has separately acknowledged that its existing drones cannot talk to each other, creating the Uncrewed Systems Centre to deal with that.
The 5th Generation Land Force programme covers the Army’s wider modernisation, including human-machine teaming and the mix of crewed and uncrewed platforms the service expects to field through the next decade.

articles.title: Moldovan President Calls Security Meeting After Massive Data Breach
articles.body:
Moldovan President Maia Sandu has called a meeting of the country's National Security Council (CNS) days after a large-scale cyberattack on government information systems.
The attack, most likely carried out with the help of artificial intelligence, resulted in the extraction of personal data belonging to approximately 750,000 Moldovans.
On October 29, Sandu's office announced that the meeting would take place in "the coming days to assess the attack and determine appropriate response measures."
The head of the country's Cybersecurity Agency, Mihai Lupascu, told RFE/RL that "without a doubt, this is the most impactful...largest cyberattack recorded so far," adding that the operation was "highly sophisticated," "well-prepared," and involved "several waves."
"We are dealing with a situation in which a highly skilled cyberactor carried out these activities with the clear objective of compromising information systems and exfiltrating data," Lupascu said.
Previously, Prime Minister Vasile Tofan told cabinet ministers that there were "indications of a broader campaign involving foreign state actors" and that investigators were looking into "their involvement in the recent incident."
He did not specify which countries were suspected of being involved.
Officials from several European nations have been warning for months of an expanding campaign of hybrid activity -- hostile actions short of open warfare, including cyberattacks, sabotage, and the weaponization of migration -- by Russia amid its war on Ukraine.
Lupascu said that while it was "premature" to definitively attribute the cyberattack to a specific actor, its complexity offered clues about who might be responsible. "At the very least, those behind it have the technical capabilities and infrastructure needed to orchestrate and carry out such attacks."
Wedged between NATO member Romania -- with which it shares close linguistic and cultural ties -- to the west and war-ravaged Ukraine to the east, Moldova has struggled to shield itself from the fallout of Moscow's full-scale invasion.
According to Moldova's Electronic Government Agency (AGE), the attack targeted about one million people, almost half of the country's population, with attempts to extract data associated with personal identification numbers (IDNPs) taking place between October 19 and October 23.
Authorities have preventively suspended 82 digital public services and disconnected over 30 information systems to limit unauthorized access, it added.
The compromised data could include identification details, such as names and dates and places of birth; information about immediate family members; health insurance status and family doctors; social benefits, pensions, and disability status; driver's license details and photographs; vehicles and companies owned or managed; and financial information, including International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs), tax debts, and payment histories.
AGE said bank card data was not affected and that no unauthorized changes were identified in state registers.
The attackers allegedly exploited vulnerabilities in services accessible without authentication, subsequently using the information obtained to attempt additional data extraction.
Authorities said security problems had been addressed in most affected services, while the remaining ones would be gradually restored once security measures had been verified. A broader review of government systems was also under way to identify and fix vulnerabilities.
AGE warned that cyberattacks pose a growing threat to public institutions, with advances in artificial intelligence making it easier to automate attacks and identify security weaknesses.
Lupascu told RFE/RL that he believed artificial intelligence was used in the latest cyberattack on Moldova, "including [capabilities] that allow the identification of vulnerabilities." He added that such tools can identify vulnerabilities "that humans cannot."
"We must be aware that artificial intelligence tools will continue to generate cyberincidents in the next few years," he warned.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Intelligence reports indicate Russia preparing new ballistic missile strikes
articles.body:
According to intelligence reports, Russia is preparing new ballistic strikes, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.
"We currently have intelligence indicating that the Russians are preparing new ballistic missile strikes. And we need the forces to shoot down all this Russian evil. We are awaiting the appropriate decisions," Zelenskyy said in an evening address on Thursday.
The president said he had chaired a meeting of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief's Headquarters, the key issue of which was countering Russian ballistic missiles.
"Sanctions pressure alone is not enough; we need the packages from our partners that we have discussed with them. If we look at key jurisdictions, sanctions can't really impose significant restrictions right away, but only over time – sometimes it takes months of work to achieve this," he said.
Zelenskyy said the longer the sanctions packages against ballistic missiles are delayed, the longer Russia will have the supply chains necessary for production.
He instructed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to expedite this work with partners.

articles.title: Russian general who ordered destruction of Skovoroda Museum to be tried in absentia
articles.body:
Russian general who ordered destruction of Skovoroda Museum to be tried in absentia
A Russian lieutenant general originally from the city of Chuhuiv in Kharkiv Oblast who is accused of directing a missile strike on the Hryhorii Skovoroda National Literary Memorial Museum will be tried in absentia.
Source: Prosecutor General's Office
Details: Regional media outlet Suspilne Kharkiv reported that the individual in question is Oleg Makovetsky, Commander of the Russian 6th Air and Air Defence Forces Army.
The investigation found that he knew full well that he was attacking a monument of Ukrainian culture rather than a military target. He issued a combat order for its destruction. Law enforcement officers have established the entire chain of transmission of the order through the commanders of the aviation division and the fighter aviation wing.
Makovetsky will be tried for violating the laws and customs of war, committed as part of a premeditated conspiracy by a group of individuals. He faces up to 15 years' imprisonment or a life sentence.
The museum in Skovorodynivka is a large memorial complex of monuments dating back to the 18th century, dedicated to the life and work of the famous Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhorii Savych Skovoroda. It was founded in 1972.
The museum collection comprises several thousand exhibits, including some of the philosopher's personal belongings, editions of his works, academic and literary works about him, books by ancient, medieval and modern philosophers and poets studied by Hryhorii Skovoroda, ethnographic artefacts, as well as paintings, graphic works and sculptures dedicated to him. Skovoroda's grave is near the main building.
Strike on the museum in Skovorodynivka
In May 2022, a Russian missile hit the roof of the building, causing a massive fire.
At that time, the missile struck beneath the roof of the building, igniting a fire that engulfed the entire museum. The 35-year-old son of the museum director, who had stayed behind to guard the premises overnight, suffered injuries. He was pulled from under the rubble and taken to hospital.
Only the statue of the philosopher survived the missile strike, becoming a distinctive symbol of resilience. Later, museum staff collected shards of pottery, metal fragments and charred books.
In 2024, the Security Service of Ukraine identified who had ordered the destruction of the Skovoroda Museum. It turned out to be Ivan Panchenko, commander of the 159th Fighter Aviation Regiment of the Western Military District of the Russian Armed Forces. Law enforcement officers notified him of the charges in absentia.
Last year, restorers managed to reconstruct 27 of the museum's exhibits.
In May 2026, a Russian drone damaged the protective shelter covering the building of the Hryhorii Skovoroda Museum.

articles.title: No seat for Europe at Ukraine peace talks – Kremlin
articles.body:
No seat for Europe at Ukraine peace talks – Kremlin
European nations will not be invited to the next Russia-US-Ukraine peace talks, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Wednesday, a day after the leaders of Finland and Norway called Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Moscow agreed in principle to participate in a fourth round of trilateral talks following last week’s meeting between Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. Mid-November has been floated as a possible timeframe, with Abu Dhabi suggested as the venue.
“We have agreed that trilateral talks will resume, involving representatives from Russia, Ukraine, and the US,” Ushakov told Vesti. He stressed, however, that European representatives will not be invited.
“They can get there if they buy tickets. But no one intends to invite them to the negotiating table.”
Ushakov’s comments came a day after Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store called Putin for a conversation that reportedly lasted over an hour. The call sent a shockwave through Kiev’s staunchest backers, prompting Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen to condemn the Nordic leaders’ initiative, insisting it had not been coordinated with “European partners.”
However, neither Stubb nor Store brought any new proposals for settling the Ukraine conflict, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the call.
Ukraine’s European backers have been excluded from all three rounds of trilateral negotiations so far and have increasingly sought direct participation in the peace process. They have, however, not tempered their demands, insisting on an unconditional ceasefire – something Moscow has repeatedly rejected, arguing that a temporary freeze to the fighting would only allow Kiev to rest and rearm with Western weapons.
Russia has also accused the EU of acting as the principal side arming Ukraine and prolonging the conflict. In April, Brussels approved €90 billion ($100 billion) to Ukraine for 2026–2027, financed via capital markets. Earlier this month, Vladimir Zelensky asked for a further €70 billion to keep Ukraine’s budget and military afloat through next year.
Moscow has maintained that Europe’s financial and military support for Ukraine makes it a party to the conflict, which Russia has long described as a NATO-led proxy war.
Putin has also described Europe’s claims of a Russian threat to justify its military buildup as “political schizophrenia.”

articles.title: Ukrainian charged over death of Monaco royal
articles.body:
Ukrainian charged over death of Monaco royal
A Ukrainian man living in Monaco has been charged in connection with the death of Antoine de Massy, a relative of Prince Albert II, the ruler of the wealthy European principality.
The 42-year-old suspect, whose identity has not been disclosed, has reportedly lived in Monaco for three decades. Prosecutor General Stephane Thibault announced a judicial investigation on Wednesday.
According to local media, the Ukrainian national has been charged with involuntary manslaughter and failure to assist a person in danger. He denies wrongdoing and has been remanded in custody.
De Massy, 29, whose father is a first cousin of Prince Albert II, was found dead on Sunday evening after apparently falling approximately 13 meters from an elevated section of the coastal Boulevard du Larvotto into a garden behind a luxury residence.
The former competitive tennis player was reportedly last seen alive overnight Saturday into Sunday, leaving a nightclub apparently intoxicated and accompanied by another man. His family alerted authorities when he failed to attend a gathering, triggering a search that led to the discovery of his body in the secluded garden.
Thibault said CCTV footage showed the suspect accompanying de Massy along Boulevard du Larvotto. The Ukrainian national was arrested on Monday, although it remains unclear whether he was the man who reportedly left the nightclub with the victim.
Earlier this year, Monaco, known as a haven for millionaires, was rocked by a bombing targeting Ukrainian-born businessman Vadim Ermolaev, who was injured alongside members of his family.
The alleged bomber was identified as a Ukrainian woman who was later found dead in her home country, reportedly killed by her handlers. Investigators identified the suspected masterminds as an active operative of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, and an unofficial agent of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU). Both are now in Ukrainian custody.
Kiev portrayed the bombing as a profit-driven crime carried out by rogue agents. However, one suspect claimed the operation had been authorized by the Ukrainian state as a legitimate act of war against Russia.
The case resurfaced this week when former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said the Monaco bombing “echoed” an alleged Ukrainian intelligence plot against him that Austrian law enforcement had thwarted.
Kravchenko fled Ukraine for Vienna last month and was subsequently dismissed by parliament after a subordinate was accused of running a protection racket on his behalf. The Austrian authorities confirmed the arrests of suspected Ukrainian intelligence operatives in early October.

articles.title: Hegseth fires Pentagon’s top military planner as Trump weighs new Iran strikes
articles.body:
Hegseth fires Pentagon’s top military planner as Trump weighs new Iran strikes
Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia ousted from the Joint Chiefs without explanation while US prepares allies for potential post-election action
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon’s top military planner, a defence official said on Wednesday, the latest in a series of generals to be ousted and one that comes even as President Donald Trump weighed renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war.
US Army Lieutentant General Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. He is the second general to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the “J5”, under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee, was forced to retire last October.
The defence official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing. The move was reported earlier by The Atlantic.

articles.title: Most Americans Believe Putin Is Stalling Ukraine Peace Talks, Back More Weapons and Sanctions, Poll Finds
articles.body:
- Category

Most Americans Believe Putin Is Stalling Ukraine Peace Talks, Back More Weapons and Sanctions, Poll Finds
A majority of American voters believe Russian leader Vladimir Putin is deliberately delaying efforts to end the war in Ukraine, while nearly two-thirds support continued military assistance to Kyiv and stronger sanctions against Moscow if Russia refuses to negotiate and prolongs the war, according to the October Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll, conducted by HarrisX.
The survey, which polled 2,700 registered US voters between October 24 and 26, 2026, is part of one of the most consistent polling series tracking American public opinion on Russia’s war against Ukraine. Its regular measurements provide insight into how attitudes toward the war and potential peace negotiations evolve over time.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The latest findings show that 68% of respondents believe Putin is stalling negotiations with the United States and Western countries rather than genuinely seeking peace, up from 61% in September. Only 32% believe the Russian leader sincerely wants to end the war.
Skepticism toward Putin extends across political affiliations, with 74% of Democrats and independent or other-party voters saying he is delaying negotiations, compared with 58% of Republicans.
By contrast, 61% of Americans believe Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy genuinely wants to end the war, while 39% think he is stalling negotiations, a slight increase from 37% in September.
Support for Zelenskyy’s stated intentions is particularly strong among Democrats, with 69% believing he is genuinely seeking peace. The same view is shared by 61% of independent or other-party voters and 52% of Republicans.
Beyond perceptions of the two leaders, the poll also indicates substantial bipartisan support for maintaining pressure on Moscow if it refuses to engage in peace negotiations.
According to the findings, 64% of Americans support continuing weapons assistance to Ukraine and imposing additional sanctions on Russia if Moscow refuses to negotiate and prolongs the war.
Notably, support for these measures is nearly identical among Republicans and Democrats, with 67% of Republican voters and 66% of Democratic voters backing continued military assistance and additional economic pressure under those circumstances.
The findings highlight an area of bipartisan agreement on US policy toward Russia’s war against Ukraine despite broader political divisions in the United States.
The survey also found growing support for direct US security guarantees for Ukraine as part of a potential peace agreement involving Ukrainian territorial concessions. Some 64% of respondents supported such an arrangement, compared with 58% in September.
However, American attitudes toward economic measures targeting Russia become more complex when domestic energy costs are taken into account.
According to the poll, 61% of Americans oppose the United States purchasing Russian oil and diesel fuel while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine, while 39% support such purchases. Opposition is particularly strong among Democrats, with 73% against buying Russian oil and diesel, compared with 64% of independent or other-party voters.
Republicans were more divided, with 54% supporting purchases of Russian oil and diesel fuel and 46% opposing them.
At the same time, 63% of respondents said they prioritize lower fuel prices over restricting Russia’s ability to finance the war, revealing a contrast between opposition to Russian energy purchases and concerns about domestic energy costs.
The findings come as diplomatic efforts to arrange further negotiations between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States continue.
A proposed trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi remains dependent on confirmation from Washington, although both Kyiv and Moscow have expressed their readiness to participate, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists on October 28.
Zelenskyy explained that the timing of the talks, expected to take place in November, could be affected by Washington’s ongoing diplomatic engagement in the Middle East.

articles.title: Bluebottle drones that never sleep level playing field in Pacific drug war
articles.body:
Australian-made Bluebottle drones to patrol Fiji's waters for drug traffickers
Fiji's hundreds of islands and vast maritime territory make it difficult to detect drug traffickers.
Intent on accessing lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand, smugglers from the Americas use the island nation as a Pacific transit point.
"Our biggest challenge is our waters are too big," Fiji's Defence Minister Pio Tikoduadua said.
"We don't even have eyes on it, let alone have the capability to affect anything on it."
But a new fleet of uncrewed maritime surface drones could help level the playing field.
The 7.4-metre-long Australian-made Bluebottles can remain at sea for up to six months, while using artificial intelligence to identify suspicious activity.
Powered by a retractable solar sail that can harness the sun and wind, they also have an underwater flipper that converts the boat's rocking in the waves into forward motion.
Mr Tikoduadua said the Bluebottles would help Fiji capitalise on its limited resources.
Traffickers are known to use yachts, fishing vessels, freight ships and even semi-submersibles, known as narco-subs.
Fiji's navy, meanwhile, operates just two large patrol boats, RFNS Savenaca and RFNS Timo, both Australian-donated Guardian-class vessels.
The RFNS Timo replaced a previous vessel, the RFNS Puamau, which ran aground during its maiden voyage in 2024.
'Virtually impossible to detect'
Australia is donating the drones and training as part of a $600 million package for the Pacific-wide Waqa Moana maritime security initiative to counter illicit drug trafficking.
The money will also fund new Australian Federal Police programs and regional surveillance support.
Fiji's first drones are expected to start arriving next year, but the total number has not been made public, with Mr Tikoduadua saying they wanted to "keep drug dealers guessing".
Australian Minister for Defence Industry and Pacific Island Affairs Pat Conroy earlier this month said the Australian Navy had 15 Bluebottles, most of which monitored the country's northern coastline, with orders in for another 40.
"They are virtually impossible to detect unless you get very close to them," he said.
An Australian company, Ocius Technology, designed the Bluebottles and operates them from a military base in Darwin.
Ocius chief growth and market development officer Rob Brezniak said the vessels could be fitted with high-tech surveillance sensors, including infrared cameras, radar and sonar to detect submarines.
He said they relayed intelligence to a team of human operators via satellite, with AI helping to filter the data and flag potential threats for a faster response.
"A government can then task an asset like a crewed vessel to approach," he said.
Mr Brezniak did not expand on how the AI technology made its assessments, saying "a combination of things helped it make an informed decision".
He also declined to disclose the individual cost of the drones, however the Australian government said its contract with Ocius to deliver the 40 drones was worth $176 million.
In Fiji's case, Mr Tikoduadua said Fijian personnel would control the Bluebottles and configure them to monitor surface vessels, with a detection range of up to 30 nautical miles (55.5km).
He said intelligence would be transmitted to human operators at the Vuvale Maritime Essential Services Centre (MESC), an Australian-funded security hub near Fiji's capital Suva which houses Fijian agencies including the navy, police and fisheries.
Mr Tikoduadua said the gathered information could be shared with partner countries and organisations if a vessel left Fiji's jurisdiction.
"If we need partner navies to come take a look, or a commercial vessel to take a look, it gives us that flexibility," he said.
Levelling the playing field
Mr Tikoduadua has seen the Bluebottles in action.
New Zealand recently deployed two to Fiji during a four-week joint operation.
Associate Professor Jose Sousa-Santos, convenor of the Pacific Regional Security Hub at the University of Canterbury in New Zealand, said officials reported the unmanned drones detected more than 100 illegal fishing vessels, many of which had switched off their transponders.
"They did exactly what they were supposed to do," he said.
"They were supported by the New Zealand Air Force and when they identified vessels that raised red flags, they were able to contact the RNZAF to provide further surveillance coverage."
Mr Sousa-Santos said the Bluebottles had the potential to disrupt trafficking operations if they were positioned in zones smugglers regularly operated in.
"It would force them to move to other trafficking routes which might not be as safe or profitable," he said.
A new frontier
Steve Symon, who chaired New Zealand's Ministerial Advisory Group on Transnational, Serious and Organised Crime, said the Bluebottles were a valuable tool.
But he feared the region's size meant they could only be effective if deployed in large numbers.
He added the crime syndicates would probably adapt.
In the short term, Mr Symon said traffickers could rely more heavily on cargo ships and corruption within ports if surveillance drones made their operations more difficult.
But it might only be a matter of time before traffickers started using similar drones, he said.
Criminal syndicates had a powerful incentive to adapt because of the huge demand for illicit drugs in Australia and New Zealand, he said.
"The reason why these [Bluebottle] drones are so good is because they are solar-powered and you can send them out for months at a time.
"But we'd be naive to think organised crime isn't going to be ready adopters of the same technology."
Sharing with Australia
Mr Tikoduadua said data the Bluebottles collected would be shared with partners, including Australia.
Mr Conroy said Australia needed to work with Fiji to stamp out the illicit drug trade, which meant "working together in a coordinated way in terms of intelligence gathering, intelligence sharing and interdiction".
Australian officials did not say whether the Bluebottles in Fiji would be used for anything beyond detecting drug traffickers and illegal fishing, such as monitoring foreign military vessels.
Jennifer Parker, an adjunct professor of defence and security at the University of Western Australia, said she did not believe the drones would have wider strategic implications for Australia's defence.
"Fiji and Australia have a significant defence partnership and we would already share significant information about what is happening in our maritime domains," she said.
"So the employment of Bluebottles to support collection of that kind of information would not be any different to, I suspect, what's already in place."

articles.title: Senior US general fired, accused of leaking classified information
articles.body:
Senior US general fired, accused of leaking classified information
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 - Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired US Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, a senior military planner on the Pentagon's Joint Staff, over accusations he leaked classified information to the public, officials said on Thursday.
Sylvia's firing is one of the highest-profile consequences to date from Hegseth's sweeping hunt for officials suspected of leaking information to the news media as the unpopular Iran war enters its ninth month.
Hegseth's effort includes a Pentagon task force to identify the source of leaks and the widespread use of polygraph exams on senior officials as part of these investigations.
Last year, he introduced a media policy that raised legal concerns among press organizations, and revoked the press credentials of journalists who refused to sign it.
A senior Pentagon official, speaking on condition of anonymity, accused Sylvia of failing three polygraphs questioning him about leaking classified information.
"The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second," the official said.
US President Donald Trump, who misidentified Sylvia as a woman, said the senior US general has "got problems."
"We're very much looking for leakers, and she's going to have big problems, long-term problems," Trump told reporters.
Sylvia could not be immediately reached for comment.
KEY POSITION
Sylvia led the Directorate for Strategy, Plans, and Policy at the Joint Staff, known inside the military as the J5, a key position that helps advise the top US military official, General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
He previously led the US Army's 101st Airborne Division. His dismissal was first reported by The Atlantic magazine.
His removal comes as the US military plans for a potential resumption of intensive bombings in Iran, something Trump has called "another little Epic Fury." The Pentagon has fumed about leaks during the Iran war, including about its planning and the expenditure of munitions.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that an internal US military analysis estimates it would cost more than $29 billion in munitions alone to restock weapons used against Iran so far. That's the bulk of the more than $47 billion spent on operations in the war.
Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, said the decision followed an extensive investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
"This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action," Parnell said, without identifying other officials who may also be targeted.
Parnell added: "Our commitment was not an empty promise. We vowed to find you, and we meant it."
A spokesperson for the Joint Staff withdrew an initial statement expressing gratitude for Sylvia's 32 years of service, saying "we determined the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances."
"Out of respect for the service member and the ongoing personnel process, we will not comment further," the spokesperson said. REUTERS

Ukrainian FPV drone operators from the Signum Battalion of the 59th Yakiv Handziuk Assault Brigade of Unmanned Systems struck Russian infantry positions in the Lyman direction, including a soldier who attempted to hide in a river.

articles.title: Russia drone strike on Ukrainian railway station kills 13
articles.body:
Russia drone strike on Ukrainian railway station kills 13
The UN’s top humanitarian official in Ukraine on Thursday condemned a Russian drone attack on the city of Dnipro that killed at least 13 civilians and injured 10 others at its main railway station.
“Civilians preparing for a trip, welcoming or bidding farewell to loved ones faced death and devastation,” said Matthias Schmale, the Humanitarian Coordinator for Ukraine, adding that displaced people and humanitarian workers at a transit centre at the station were left in shock by the nearby explosions.
Media outlets reported that a jet-powered drone hit the station as a train due to travel to Zaporizhzhia stood at a platform. An 11-year-old boy was among the injured, according to regional officials cited in the reports.
Rising risks for rail passengers
Mr. Schmale expressed condolences to the families of those killed on behalf of the UN, noting that train travel is a key means of transportation in Ukraine.
Since the start of the year, he said, travellers and railway workers have faced increased risks on every journey due to Russian military strikes and air alerts affecting the safety and reliability of trains.
According to figures from Ukraine’s railway operator cited by media outlets, attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
Recent months have seen repeated attacks across the country on civilian infrastructure critical to daily life, including bridges, hospitals, schools, shopping centres and railway stations, Mr. Schmale said.
Inured to violence
“The images from Dnipro cannot become another story that fades from attention. Behind every casualty is a person, a family and a future changed forever,” he said.
“It cannot be repeated often enough that civilians and civilian infrastructure are protected under international humanitarian law.”
Aid convoys head for Oleshky
Mr. Schmale told UN News in an interview on Thursday that preparations to get aid into Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Kherson region, were “accelerating” while a local ceasefire held, and that deliveries could arrive as early as Friday.
The ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump and announced by the White House on 23 October, is due to end on the evening of 1 November.
Ukraine’s Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets, has said he is on his way to the town and will accompany residents out.
Mr. Schmale said mined roads were a key reason residents had been trapped. He pointed to images of a stretch known locally as the “road of death”.
“It’s clear any safe passage both in and out has to have mine clearance preceding it,” he said, adding that reports reaching him confirmed demining was under way.
Offer of support ‘not taken up’
The UN has no direct role in the evacuation. “We have offered support, but it’s not been taken up,” Mr. Schmale said, adding that none of its partners were involved either.
Under established procedure, evacuees will get help once they reach Government-controlled areas.
That includes food and other material assistance, and possibly help finding housing. “There’s a high likelihood that we will get involved the minute they are here,” he said.
More than 1,000 likely to remain
Mr. Schmale said estimates varied, but he had heard that 200 to 300 people might leave, “which would leave more than 1,000 there, and they would need support”.
He cited accounts from UN human rights monitors, civil society groups and the Ukrainian authorities.
The town’s remaining health facility was “barely functional” and short of medicine, he said, and keeping warm through winter amid energy disruption would be a growing challenge. Safe water and public infrastructure were also pressing needs.
“Because they’ve been trapped in that place for so long under heavy bombardment, mental health issues should never be overlooked,” he said.

articles.title: Pentagon fires top military planner
articles.body:
Pentagon fires top military planner
The Pentagon has fired its top military strategist as Washington draws up contingency plans for a possible escalation of hostilities with Iran.
Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia has been removed from his position as director for strategy, plans, and policy (J5) on the Joint Staff, a spokesman confirmed late Wednesday, following media reports of his dismissal.
His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced into retirement a year ago amid reported friction with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine. Sylvia previously served as vice director of the J5.
The Pentagon did not explain Sylvia’s departure. His responsibilities included developing military strategies and plans to advise the chairman and the US president. He joins nearly two dozen senior military and civilian officials removed during Hegseth’s tenure.
The secretary has portrayed the dismissals as part of an effort to reduce the military’s bloated ranks of generals and make the armed forces more efficient and lethal. Critics, however, have characterized the shake-up as an ideological “purge.”
President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of renewing large-scale hostilities with Iran, including resuming the intensive bombing campaign conducted during the first 40 days of the conflict, which the US and Israel launched in late February. A potential escalation could be timed around the November midterm elections.
Military experts have widely expressed concern that another bombing campaign would fail to “finish the job,” as Trump has put it, while further increasing the conflict’s economic toll worldwide. Tehran has repeatedly warned that it is prepared to retaliate against US allies in the Gulf region if it faces renewed attacks.
Conversely, speculation has emerged that Trump could dismiss Hegseth after the midterms, when the opposition Democratic Party is expected to make gains in both chambers of Congress. Critics of the Iran war, including Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, have argued that firing the secretary could help Trump avoid a potential impeachment battle if Democrats take control of the House.
Trump’s public rhetoric remains supportive of Hegseth and his policies.

articles.title: Early warning radar flown on Protector type airframe
articles.body:
General Atomics and Saab have flown an airborne early warning radar on an uncrewed MQ-9B, the same aircraft the Royal Air Force operates as Protector, tracking fighter jets and commercial aircraft along with maritime targets at long range during months of testing, according to the companies.
The flights used a Saab LoyalEye radar carried in payload pods on a General Atomics MQ-9B operating from the company’s Desert Horizon facility in southern California, and demonstrated simultaneous tracking of several airborne and maritime targets, including multiple instrumented fighter jets acting as targets.
David Alexander, president of General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, said: “This has been one of the most highly anticipated flight tests we have performed. The level of customer interest in AEW capability on MQ-9B throughout the world is extremely high. It just makes sense.”
Carl-Johan Bergholm, head of Saab’s surveillance business area, said: “This flight test underscores Saab’s commitment to evolving airborne early warning capabilities to meet future operational needs. LoyalEye complements existing capabilities by adding flexibility, extending reach, and enabling a more efficient use of resources in demanding environments.”
Airborne early warning has always meant a large crewed aircraft, because the radar, the operators and the fuel to stay up all demanded size, and the number any air force can afford has fallen with every generation. Britain is buying three Wedgetail aircraft to replace a Sentry fleet that once numbered seven. The Royal Air Force will hold one of the smallest early warning forces of any major air arm.
Putting the radar on an uncrewed aircraft changes the arithmetic of that problem, because an MQ-9B can stay airborne far longer than a crewed jet, costs a fraction as much to buy and operate, and risks nobody if it is lost. What it cannot do is carry the battle management staff who make a Wedgetail more than a big flying radar, so the companies describe the command and control function being performed elsewhere, on the ground, on a ship or aboard an existing crewed aircraft, etc.
Protector entered Royal Air Force service at RAF Waddington this year, replacing Reaper, and ministers confirmed this month that eleven of the sixteen aircraft on order have been delivered. The type is certified to fly in civil airspace. Earlier armed drones were not, and that certification is why Protector can fly over Britain.
General Atomics is also developing a short take-off and landing version of the MQ-9B intended to operate from aircraft carriers, a configuration the Royal Navy has watched closely as it works out what flies from HMS Prince of Wales and HMS Queen Elizabeth alongside the F-35B.
Saab’s existing airborne early warning radars fly on the GlobalEye, based on the Bombardier Global 6000 business jet, which Sweden operates and which has been sold to the United Arab Emirates and ordered by Denmark.

articles.title: Baltic state plans universal conscription
articles.body:
Baltic state plans universal conscription
Lithuania will introduce universal male conscription despite public resistance to compulsory military service, the country’s government has announced.
The Baltic state reinstated selective conscription in 2015, seven years after abolishing it. Under the new plan, the draft would be extended to all eligible men, while women would continue to serve voluntarily.
Annual recruitment will increase from just over 5,000 to around 7,500 men, President Gitanas Nauseda announced on Thursday following a State Defense Council meeting.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius described universal conscription as “necessary and inevitable.”
The decision follows similar recruitment pushes elsewhere in Europe. Poland is considering restoring compulsory service, which was abolished in 2009, and introducing a system covering both men and women. A recent poll, however, found that 53% of Poles aged 18–24 opposed reinstatement of the draft.
Germany has already introduced mandatory military registration for 18-year-old men. Enlistment remains voluntary, but parliament can activate compulsory service if recruitment falls short or the security situation deteriorates.
Berlin’s recruitment drive has met resistance, with some 45,000 people joining student protests across roughly 100 German cities and towns in September, with some carrying banners reading “We won’t fight in your wars” and “Russia is not our enemy.”
Applications for conscientious objector status reached over 12,000 between January and August, compared with 3,879 throughout 2025, according to figures reported by German media.
European officials have nevertheless continued discussing preparations for a possible war with Russia by the end of the decade. Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem “joked” last month that if Estonia mobilized and Russia did not attack, it would be “economically more correct to attack ourselves” rather than keep troops waiting.
Moscow has repeatedly stated that it has neither reason nor intention to attack NATO countries, describing such allegations as “horror stories” intended to prepare European populations for further militarization.
Russian officials have warned that Europe’s military buildup could itself lead to confrontation and that expanding NATO infrastructure near Russia’s borders would prompt additional security measures. Moscow has stressed that it is prepared to defend itself if attacked.

articles.title: Naval drones sink Greek container ship sailing from Israel off Bulgaria's coast
articles.body:
A Greek-owned container ship chartered by Israeli shipping company ZIM sank in the Black Sea after being struck by unmanned surface vessels off the coast of Bulgaria on Wednesday, Bulgarian authorities said, in the latest attack on commercial shipping amid growing concerns over the spillover effects of the Russia-Ukraine war.
The Liberian-flagged CONTSHIP JET was carrying 421 shipping containers from Haifa's Gulf Port in Israel to the Romanian port of Constanța when it was attacked while passing through Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, outside the country's territorial waters.
All 18 crew members, including 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians, were rescued and safely transported to the Bulgarian port of Varna.
The Bulgarian government said it had received advance warning of the attack, believed to be connected to the war between Russia and Ukraine, but was unable to prevent it.
Footage published by a Bulgarian news website showed one of the unmanned surface vessels approaching the container ship moments before impact.
The ship sustained severe damage in the attack and subsequently sank, according to Bulgarian authorities.
The identity of those responsible remains unclear. Initial assessments suggest the vessel was not targeted because of its connection to Israel, although investigators have yet to establish a motive.
The incident has heightened concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in the western Black Sea, where attacks involving aerial and maritime drones have become increasingly frequent.
At least six vessels have been attacked by aerial or unmanned surface drones off Bulgaria's coast this month, leaving approximately 25 people dead, according to reports. The attacks have raised fears that the conflict between Russia and Ukraine is increasingly threatening shipping routes beyond the immediate war zone.
ZIM confirmed that the damaged vessel was chartered by the company but was not part of its owned fleet.
"A small container ship carrying a limited number of containers, which ZIM charters but does not own, was struck by an unmanned surface vessel in the Black Sea," the company said in a statement.
"All crew members were safely evacuated, and the expected financial damage, according to a preliminary assessment, is minimal."
The company said it was working to secure a replacement vessel and maintain service to its customers.
"To the best of our knowledge, several similar incidents involving vessels in the area have occurred over the past month," ZIM added.
Oren Caspi, chairman of ZIM's workers' union, said the attack underscored the importance of maintaining Israeli control over the shipping company amid growing geopolitical instability.
"In a reality of boycotts and security threats, in a world of political instability, we must keep ZIM Israeli," Caspi said.
"Much remains unknown about this extraordinary attack, and we are still learning the details."
Although Bulgaria does not share a land border with Russia or Ukraine, its position on the western Black Sea places it along important commercial shipping routes connecting the region to major Russian and Ukrainian ports.
The Black Sea has become a key theater of the Russia-Ukraine war, with unmanned aerial vehicles and explosive-laden maritime drones increasingly used in attacks on naval and maritime targets.
Such incidents have become more frequent in recent months, affecting Eastern European countries and shipping corridors previously considered relatively secure.
At least 45 merchant vessels have been attacked over the past 12 months in parts of the Black Sea that had not previously been classified as high-risk areas, according to figures cited in the report.
The latest sinking highlights the growing risks facing civilian shipping in the region, where commercial vessels continue to operate amid an expanding threat from unmanned weapons.
While there is no indication that the CONTSHIP JET was targeted because of its Israeli commercial connection, the attack adds to concerns among shipping operators about the safety of Black Sea routes and the potential for further disruption to international trade.

articles.title: Exclusive-First Russian diesel from Putin-Trump deal heading for US, data shows
articles.body:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.
Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US midterm elections.
Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.
The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7. The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known.
Post publication, Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Limited (EASTMED), the manager of the Agioi Fanendes tanker, said that the vessel was awaiting orders while sailing towards the North Atlantic but its destination had not been determined as New York.
“The discharging port or country is not yet nominated and finalised,” an EASTMED official told Reuters.
The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.
Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.
A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.
“As far as I’m aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.
The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.
RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTSSince the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.
It also supplies Central Asia by rail.
Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.
It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, LSEG data showed.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.
Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.
That account was not accurate, a source familiar with the matter said.
Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end.
(Reporting by Reuters; editing by Philippa Fletcher, Jason Neely and Jon Boyle)

articles.title: Israel’s Smart Shooter exports drone-killing weapon station to Asia
articles.body:
- Smart Shooter delivered the first batch of SMASH Hopper MG remote weapon stations to an integrator building a defense system for an Asian military.
- The systems will support counter-drone and ground defense, and Smart Shooter helped set up local installation and maintenance capability.
Israeli company Smart Shooter has delivered the first batch of its SMASH Hopper MG remote weapon stations to an unnamed integrator in Asia, which is building them into a defense system for an Asian military to shoot down drones and engage ground targets, the company said on social media.
Smart Shooter did not identify the country, the armed force or the integrator, and it did not say how many systems were in the first batch, what the contract is worth or when further deliveries will follow. As part of the project, the company also helped the customer set up local installation and maintenance capability.
The SMASH Hopper is a lightweight remotely operated weapon station that lets a soldier aim and fire from behind cover or from inside a vehicle, and the MG designation refers to the version configured for a machine gun. It uses Smart Shooter’s SMASH fire control technology, which tracks a moving target and releases the shot only when the computer calculates a hit, an approach the company built for hitting small drones that are hard to engage with ordinary iron sights or optics.
Earlier SMASH Hopper versions carried an assault rifle, including the configuration inside the company’s SMASH DOME portable counter-drone system, which pairs the weapon station with radar and optical sensors.
Israel Defense Forces units have used the SMASH Hopper for several years, Smart Shooter said in June, when Israel’s Defense Ministry placed a new order worth up to $2.5 million with delivery by the end of 2026. That followed a separate ministry contract in May for SMASH Hopper systems, spare parts and services, which Israeli media linked to the drone threat on the country’s northern border.
Most of Smart Shooter’s sales come from its rifle-mounted SMASH 2000L and SMASH 3000 fire control sights, which are used by U.S. forces, and in September the U.S. Army included the company’s U.S. subsidiary in a group of 10 counter-drone suppliers sharing $4.15 billion in contracts, with Smart Shooter receiving $150 million. The company says the SMASH family is also used in Britain, Germany and other NATO countries.
Smart Shooter described the Asian integrator’s system as a layered defense against threats in the air and on the ground, but it did not say which other sensors or weapons the system includes or when the armed force expects to put it into service.

articles.title: Pentagon treating military base freezer malfunctions as suspected cyberattack, officials say
articles.body:
Pentagon treating military base freezer malfunctions as suspected cyberattack, officials say
- The Pentagon is treating freezer failures at US military bases as a suspected cyberattack. Investigators are working with Cyber Command, law enforcement, and French counterparts.
- At least six commissaries were hit in late August. In one case at Fort Huachuca, the freezer “went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food”.
- The case raises wider fears about hacked cold storage. A similar French attack hit over 350 sites, caused major food losses, and showed outdated controllers can be easy targets.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US Pentagon is treating the spate of mysterious freezer malfunctions that spoilt food at military bases across the United States in August as a suspected hack, according to four officials familiar with the matter.
One of the officials said the military investigators were in touch with their French counterparts about a similar cyberattack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets there earlier in October.
Reuters was unable to ascertain how far along the Pentagon’s investigation was or whether it had reached any conclusions about what happened or who might be responsible.
When asked about the investigation, the Pentagon said that a unit of Cyber Command – the military’s cyber force – was “working in close coordination with interagency and law enforcement partners”. It did not elaborate.
The US Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division said its Cyber Field Office was involved in the investigation and that it was working with French law enforcement to better understand “the refrigeration outages in Europe”.
The late August malfunctions in the United States affected at least six commissaries – on-base stores where military personnel buy their food – according to a Reuters review of the military bases’ contemporaneous Facebook posts and website updates.
In at least one of the cases, the freezers did not simply stop working; the cooling units’ temperatures were cranked up overnight, yielding mounds of wilted or melted food in the morning.
The Fort Huachuca, Arizona Facebook account explained on Aug 26 that its freezer “went into defrost mode where it heated up all the food. Trust us when we say it was ‘spoiled’”.
The spate of rogue freezer behaviour and the possibility of cyber-sabotage were first reported on Aug 28 by a recently created blog called Signal and Silence.
The involvement of military investigators and their contacts with the French were reported by the newspaper Stars and Stripes and Britain’s Daily Telegraph, respectively. The news that the investigators were treating the incident as a suspected hack was first reported by Reuters.
The French Embassy in Washington said it would have no comment.
French freezers fried
If confirmed to be a cyberattack, the refrigerator malfunctions would be another illustration of how vulnerable critical infrastructure – in this case cold storage – can be to hackers.
The French freezer cyberattack overrode the temperature controls on commercial cooling units in more than 350 establishments, leading to dramatic scenes as supermarkets’ frozen food aisles were cleared of spoilt merchandise.
The French hack involved cranking the temperature inside the units up rather than merely knocking them offline, similar to what happened in Fort Huachuca in Arizona. Some French refrigeration units had the temperature turned up so high they caught fire.
The French attack’s total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, one supermarket owner estimated earlier in October.
The French cyberattack appeared to have been easy to pull off, experts previously told Reuters. The Danish firm Danfoss, whose controllers ran many of the stricken units, said that many of the devices were obsolete or were running outdated firmware, which could have made it easy for hackers to break in.
Reuters could not establish whether Danfoss or any other brand of freezer controller were in use at the affected US bases. Danfoss did not return messages seeking comment.
Chilling hacks
Refrigeration plays a critical role in the distribution of fresh food and the sabotage of cold storage facilities over the internet has long been seen as a nightmare scenario, alongside the loss of electricity or water plants.
Earlier in 2026, the Global Food Safety Initiative, an industry body, called on food safety professionals and IT leaders to work together to ensure “robust cybersecurity” for refrigeration technology, noting that “a hacked cooling system is just as dangerous as a broken one”.
Hackers have previously sabotaged fridges and freezers both in the US and elsewhere.
Danfoss has said that, in 2022, hackers either targeted or broke into supermarkets in Russia and Israel that were using obsolete versions of its cold storage controllers.
In December 2025, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles accused a Ukrainian woman of being part of a hacker group that knocked out the refrigeration at a meatpacking facility in 2024, ruining more than 900kg of meat.
The root problem was that controllers that were initially conceived as isolated interfaces that would be serviced by an in-person technician were increasingly being connected to the internet, said Bill Moore, the chief executive of industrial cybersecurity firm Xona Systems.
Concerns about online exposure were not unique to cooling systems, he said, but they could have particularly serious consequences there.
“It can definitely disrupt the supply chain for food,” he said. REUTERS
