articles.title: Demining complete, humanitarian convoy ready: Oleshky mission advances as ceasefire holds and Lubinets heads to occupied city
articles.body:
Ukraine’s humanitarian mission to Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has reached a key stage, with mine clearance along designated routes completed and a humanitarian convoy ready to depart, Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said on 29 October.
The mission aims to deliver humanitarian aid to civilians trapped in the occupied city facing humanitarian crisis, and provide a safe way out for those who want to leave. The operation is taking place under a localized ceasefire coordinated with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump.
Lubinets said the ceasefire has held for 54 hours without reported violations.
Aid convoy prepared, civilian evacuations planned
Lubinets said the humanitarian convoy was ready to leave and was expected to reach Oleshky’s central hospital. Residents would receive the assistance they need, he said.
Civilians wishing to leave the city would have an opportunity to do so until 2 p.m. local time, with security measures organized for their departure. Distribution of humanitarian aid was scheduled to begin after 2:30 p.m.
Delegations from Ukraine, Russia, and the United States had gathered to coordinate the next steps in the mission. Journalists from all three countries were also present, Lubinets said.
Lubinets travels to occupied Oleshky
Earlier on 29 October, Lubinets said he was still traveling toward Oleshky.
He said he wanted to be on the ground to see the situation firsthand and report on the mission’s progress. Lubinets also asked the public to rely on official sources and wait until he returned before raising further questions about the negotiations.
The Ukrainian ombudsman said the negotiations had been difficult and lengthy, adding that the mission had reached only the halfway point toward its goals.
“If I had to go for the sake of one person, I would go again,” Lubinets said, describing the mission as his duty to help Ukrainians in need.
US-mediated ceasefire enables humanitarian operation
The mission is being conducted jointly by Lubinets and Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova, with mediation and coordination by Melania Trump.
The localized ceasefire took effect on 27 October to allow mine clearance, humanitarian deliveries, and civilian evacuations.
Oleshky, on the east bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, has been under Russian occupation since 2022. Russian occupation and restrictions on access to the city have left civilians facing severe shortages of food, medicine, and other essential supplies, while access to medical care has become increasingly difficult. The humanitarian mission aims to deliver urgently needed aid and help residents who want to leave reach safety.
Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
Lubinets thanked Melania Trump and the Ukrainians and US citizens who helped bring attention to the situation in Oleshky and support the negotiations. He said the mission’s priority remained delivering assistance and helping civilians leave safely.

articles.title: The Guardian view on a changing Brexit debate: Kemi Badenoch is trapped in denial | Editorial
articles.body:
British politics is still polarised around Brexit, although 10 years on from the referendum, the terms of debate are very different. Or they should be. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has moved discussions of European solidarity from the realm of abstraction to a matter of urgent defence partnership. Donald Trump’s presidency in the US, marked by scorn for European democracies and indulgence of Vladimir Putin, has undermined confidence that Britain can rely on any “special relationship” with Washington.
Under these circumstances, it would be absurd to deny that a reappraisal of Brexit is in order. The prime minister acknowledged this in his speech at the Labour party conference last month, calling for a national conversation about the future relationship with every option, including rejoining, on the table. The Eurosceptic opposition are having none of it. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accuses the government of stirring division by raising the European question. She told MPs this week that Labour should thank the Tories for the Brexit deal they negotiated.
The Tories and Reform UK like to remind Andy Burnham of comments he made when campaigning in Makerfield earlier this year for the seat that became his launchpad to reach No 10. Mr Burnham said that rerunning the old Brexit arguments was “the last thing we should do right now”. That can be made consistent with his current position in the sense that an exact rerun of the 2016 debate would indeed be pointless, which is why something different, more future-facing, is being proposed instead. Mr Burnham’s critics see that as sleight of hand to conceal a flagrant change of line. But the distinction between relitigating outdated arguments and engaging with present realities is a vital one.
The Tory position, shared with Reform, contains no audit of Britain’s foreign and economic policy interests. It is based on ideology and fear of confronting the facts that such an evaluation reveals. Brexit has made Britain poorer and diminished its influence on the world stage. The public know this all too well, as evidenced by opinion polls indicating majority support for a closer EU relationship.
Mrs Badenoch’s position is also disingenuous, given her commitment to pull Britain out of the European convention on human rights. That would pointlessly reopen some of the most fissile Brexit arguments because of the ECHR’s codification in the Good Friday agreement for Northern Ireland.
A phenomenon that Mrs Badenoch and Mr Burnham have observed, but respond to differently, is that voters have no desire for a return to the poisonous political atmosphere of the immediate post-referendum period. The Tory leader uses that aversion to justify her lack of a strategic concept for Britain’s future relationship with its continental neighbours. The prime minister’s approach is to sound ecumenical, saying that he aspires to national consensus on the best way forward, while sounding vague about his personal preferences.
That ambiguity has given the opposition cause to accuse the prime minister of conspiring to undo Brexit, but it has also dissolved some of the taboo around discussion of much closer models of reintegration with the EU, which is a necessary condition for a healthier fact-based debate. That isn’t a conversation the Conservatives want to have, but for the prime minister to share in their denial would be, as he has said, a dereliction of duty.

articles.title: Iran says four tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran says four tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz
At least four tankers have caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to navigate the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's armed forces said Thursday, a day after the US military said it had cleared key routes through the waterway.
"Over the past 24 hours, three violating oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking mines while attempting to pass through the unauthorised southern route of the Strait of Hormuz," Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement.
The vessels had "switched off all their radar and navigation systems" and disregarded warnings from the IRGC navy, the statement said.
It was not immediately clear when the incidents occurred or which flags the tankers were flying.
Later Thursday, Iran's army reported that another tanker had caught fire east of the strait.
"A tanker that was illegally operating in a restricted and dangerous area east of the Strait of Hormuz was damaged and caught fire after striking naval mines, rendering it unable to move," the army said in a statement carried by state television.
The British maritime agency UKMTO, meanwhile, said it had received a report of a ship on fire in the strait.
"Regional authorities have identified the vessel as a dhow, which was involved in a maritime security incident, igniting a large fire onboard causing the dhow to list and sink," it said.
"The crew have been safely evacuated."
In recent weeks, Iran has reported multiple vessels striking sea mines, prompting US Central Command (CENTCOM), which runs military operations in the region, to reaffirm on social media its insistence that all mines in "primary transit routes" have been cleared.
On Thursday, Hossein Mohebi, the spokesman for the IRGC challenged the claim, saying: "Prove your Hormuz mine-clearing claim with independent evidence, not statements!" in a post on X.
Since the outbreak of the war on 28 February, Iran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.
The United States has in response imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and helped tankers travel the strait. On Sunday CENTCOM said it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.
Iran considers ships using the southern corridor near the Omani coast unauthorised.
In their statement on Thursday, the Guards said "the IRGC Navy states that the unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz is mined, and that vessel owners and crews are responsible for transiting these routes and should not pay attention to CENTCOM's delusions on social media".
The IRGC also said it had captured a US reconnaissance drone, in a separate statement.
"The IRGC Navy announced that its electronic warfare unit had successfully captured a US MQM-170 drone during an offensive operation in the western Strait of Hormuz," the statement said.
(AFP)

‘Back up!’ US ambassador erupts at Cuban minister (VIDEO)
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz shouted “Back up!” at Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez during a heated confrontation at the General Assembly over Washington’s blockade of the island. The Cuban diplomat accused Waltz of spreading “crude lies” to justify US “economic aggression.”
During the UNGA session on Tuesday, Waltz dedicated his speech to allegations of corruption among the Cuban leadership, pointing to what he called their collection of luxury watches, real estate, and yachts, as well as their relatives’ holidays in Europe. While ordinary Cubans “are starving,” the US blockade and embargo of the island “does not exist” and “doesn’t apply to luxury goods” that “somehow get through to the Cuban regime elites,” he claimed.
His words drew loud condemnation from the Cuban delegation led by Rodriguez as the diplomats clapped and knocked on their desks in protest against Waltz’s speech.
See the corrupt Cuban regime’s Rolex collection while their people sit in the dark. https://t.co/6wMlNhmNhl
— Ambassador Mike Waltz (@USAmbUN) October 27, 2026
The foreign minister interrupted the US diplomat’s speech by requesting urgent intervention and delivered his own remarks, in which he accused the American envoy of lying in a “rude and arrogant manner” and “violating the dignity of the General Assembly” with his words.
Rodriguez approached the podium and engaged in a heated argument with Waltz. In a video posted on X by the US envoy, Waltz is heard urging the General Assembly president to make the Cuban minister “back away from this podium,” saying he would not allow Rodriguez to “intimidate” him on US territory. He shouted: “I’m the representative of the United States of America! Back up! […] Do you understand who you are dealing with?! Back up!”
The Castro regime has profited at the expense of the Cuban people with luxury cars, expensive watches and a private island resort. As I shared this with the world, regime thugs rushed the stage to interrupt my speech. They can intimidate their own people in Cuba but think again about trying that nonsense in the United States of America.
— Ambassador Mike Waltz (@USAmbUN) October 27, 2026
The US ambassador posted videos on social media detailing the incident, accusing the “so-called ‘diplomats’” and “regime thugs” of “melting down at the first hint of criticism.”
Rodriguez subsequently addressed the General Assembly, accusing Waltz of lying in a “rude and arrogant manner” and “violating the dignity of the General Assembly” with his remarks.
He later shared a cartoon on X depicting the confrontation with the words “Gringo mentiroso” (lying gringo) above the two diplomats. He captioned the post: “Cuba is not a threat. The blockade is.”
#CubaNoEsUnaAmenaza El Bloqueo Sí. https://t.co/OJd5pcHKBQ
— Bruno Rodríguez P (@BrunoRguezP) October 28, 2026
In a separate post, Rodriguez “denounced the economic war that the United States is waging against Cuba with aims of domination and ‘regime change.’” Rodriguez blasted the blockade as an “act of war” and “genocide prohibited by the International Law.” He also shared the results of the vote, which he said was rejected by a “large majority” of the nations.
A resolution condemning the US embargo of Cuba was supported by 130 countries, including Russia, China, India, and even several US allies such as Canada, France, and the UK. It was opposed by 17 nations, including the US, Israel, and Ukraine, with 25 nations abstaining.
US President Donald Trump has intensified pressure on Havana since the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. Trump has since repeatedly stated that Cuba would be “next,” as his administration imposed a near-total energy blockade against the island nation.
The restrictions contributed to severe energy shortages on the island. Cuba has entered its worst economic crisis in decades, marked not only by prolonged blackouts but also food shortages. Last month, Trump described Cuba as an “absolutely failed state” and “a haven for foreign adversaries” on America’s doorstep.
Moscow and Beijing have expressed solidarity with Cuba in the face of the pressure. Russia has been among the countries providing relief to Cuba, delivering around 700,000 barrels of oil in March. China also said in late September it would support Cuba in “safeguarding its national sovereignty” and pursuing a “development path suited to its national conditions.”
In mid-October, the US issued an arrest warrant for former Cuban President Raul Castro, 95, accusing him of ordering an attack on two American planes operated by anti-Communist Cuban exiles off the island’s coast in 1996. The warrant followed a separate federal indictment brought against Castro and five others in May. Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel condemned the case as a “political maneuver, devoid of any legal foundation” and accused Washington of creating a pretext for a military intervention.
Moscow has condemned the accusations against the former Cuban leader as “groundless” and “contrived,” calling it “revenge” by the anti-Cuban lobby.

articles.title: Anger in Syria over govt 'inaction' after Jordanian airstrikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Anger in Syria over government 'inaction' after deadly Jordanian airstrikes
Many Syrians have expressed anger at their government following its response to deadly Jordanian airstrikes in southern Syria, criticising it for its lack of action and appearing to accept Amman’s justification for an operation that killed civilians, including children.
Jordan’s military said Monday that its air force had struck what it described as terrorist sites in the southern Syrian province of Daraa, targeting groups it said were linked to a deadly shooting at a church in southern Jordan which killed nine people on 23 October, a rare incident in the kingdom. Jordanian authorities said they arrested three suspects behind the shooting.
The Islamic State (IS) group later claimed responsibility for the shooting. Jordanian officials subsequently claimed that the attack in southern Syria had killed more than 20 IS members and targeted a major weapons depot, while acknowledging unintended civilian casualties.
While Jordan has carried out repeated airstrikes in southern Syria in recent years, primarily against drug-smuggling networks operating near its border, Monday's operation has fuelled particular outrage because of the civilian toll and questions over whether Damascus had agreed to the strikes.
Amman said the operation was coordinated with the Syrian government, a claim Damascus rejected, saying the strikes were carried out without prior notification or coordination.
The Syrian Foreign Ministry condemned the attacks as a violation of the country’s sovereignty, said an investigation had been launched and called for coordination over security operations along the shared border.
However, criticism intensified after Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and his Jordanian counterpart, Ayman al-Safadi, issued a joint statement on Wednesday following a telephone call to discuss the consequences of the strikes.
The statement said Safadi had explained that the operation was based on field intelligence and aimed at "neutralising confirmed threats and imminent terrorist operations targeting Jordan's security." He also expressed regret over civilian deaths.
The two sides agreed to establish a joint security committee to examine the circumstances and repercussions of the strikes and strengthen coordination along the border.
Although Damascus had separately condemned the operation and summoned Jordan’s ambassador to deliver a formal protest, many Syrians have viewed the joint statement as accepting Jordan’s account.
Comments online, including under the Syrian Foreign Ministry’s statement on X, have reflected widespread anger over what users described as the government’s failure to defend Syrian sovereignty and adequately respond to the civilian deaths.
"Are these the ISIS members, Minister? And are these ISIS weapons depots, Your Excellency?" one user wrote, questioning Jordan’s account while referring to images showing the aftermath of the strikes and child victims.
Others argued that accepting Jordan’s justification for the operation could provide Israel with further excuses to widen its occupation in southern Syria under the pretext of fighting extremist groups.
After Assad’s fall, Israel invaded Syria’s Quneitra and Mount Hermon regions, claiming its military presence there was needed to prevent extremist militants from reaching its border.
"You are completely unfit for this position. How can you allow the Jordanian king to use you to push this narrative, while you repeat it so blindly?" one user wrote, addressing Syrian officials.
"Do not complain when Israeli forces invade Daraa under the pretext of rooting out ISIS. You are officially acknowledging that ISIS is present there, and you have now given Israel the green light," the user added.
Another comment accused the government of accepting Jordan’s account at the expense of the victims.
"A statement full of humiliation, submission and acceptance of the Jordanian narrative. It also betrays the blood of those killed by describing the massacre as a strike against terrorists. Were the children terrorists?" the user wrote.
The criticism reflects wider sensitivities and concerns in southern Syria, where residents have faced years of conflict, repeated Israeli incursions and security operations. Many remain under threat of foreign military action in Syria, which often kills civilians.
IS controlled large swathes of Syria before its territorial defeat in 2019, but the group continues to operate clandestine cells, particularly in desert areas, and has claimed attacks against security forces and civilians.
The group's continued activity has raised concerns about the future of counterterrorism operations as the US reduces its military presence in Syria.

articles.title: Russian military clears mines for Melania Trump’s aid mission (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russian military clears mines for Melania Trump’s aid mission (VIDEO)
The Russian military is intensifying efforts to clear mines and unexploded ordnance from roads leading to a Ukrainian town where a local ceasefire was announced this week to allow a humanitarian mission mediated by US First Lady Melania Trump.
The proposed aid deliveries are intended to alleviate the dire conditions facing residents trapped in Alyoshki due to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
Footage released by the Russian Defense Ministry on Thursday shows a Russian mine-clearing robot and its operators securing access to the town in the Russian region of Kherson, which Ukraine still claims. Most of the munitions being disposed of are foreign-made, one of the explosives specialists said.
The ministry explained that many of the explosive devices discovered in the area originated in Western countries and were being detonated on-site to accelerate the clearance operation.
Russian President Vladimir Putin addressed the humanitarian effort during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, saying: “We are working on this, just as we are working to resolve the Ukraine conflict.” He accused Ukrainian forces of bringing Alyoshki to the brink of a “humanitarian disaster” by blockading the town, a situation the US first lady is seeking to alleviate.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also credited Melania Trump for helping negotiate the ceasefire, saying the breakthrough built on earlier humanitarian cooperation. The first lady has been closely involved in efforts to reunite Russian and Ukrainian children separated from their families during the conflict, the official added.
The Alyoshki operation is supported by the Belarusian government, which is providing logistical assistance to the foreign officials involved. On Thursday morning, local media filmed Russian and Ukrainian delegations departing together from the Belarusian city of Gomel.
Russian human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova thanked her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmitry Lubinets, and Melania Trump for helping advance the humanitarian mission.
“Our main goal is to deliver aid to those who are staying in the town. We will also give a chance to anyone who wants to leave Alyoshki,” she wrote on social media. “The important part now is to reach people and provide for their needs.”

Earlier Thursday, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense issued emergency warnings in Riyadh, the Al-Kharj governorate in central Saudi Arabia, and the southern city of Najran through the National Early Warning Platform.
Minutes later, the agency announced that the danger had passed, urging residents to continue following safety instructions and avoid gathering or filming.
Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi missile and drone attacks amid an escalation in the conflict in neighboring Yemen.

Russia’s Military Losses Hit All-Time Monthly High as Ukraine Reports Over 49,000 in October
Russian military personnel losses in October 2026 have reached 49,040 as of October 29, marking the highest monthly figure since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The General Staff reported that the previous monthly record was registered in December 2024, when Russian forces suffered 48,670 personnel losses.
With October still underway, Russia’s average daily personnel losses have reached approximately 1,750, according to Ukrainian military estimates.
The figures also indicate a substantial increase in Russian losses over recent months. In February 2026, Russian forces sustained an estimated 26,090 personnel losses, compared with 46,230 in September and 49,040 as of October 29.
“Why this matters: The rate of Russian personnel losses exceeds the military’s ability to replenish its units. Each month of the war is becoming increasingly costly for Russia’s armed forces,” the General Staff added.
Ukrainian drone strikes have killed or wounded more than 302,000 Russian military personnel since the beginning of 2026, averaging over 1,000 casualties per day in less than ten months, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported on October 27.
March recorded the highest number of Russian personnel casualties from Ukrainian drone strikes, with 33,989 soldiers killed or wounded. April followed with 33,961 casualties, while February saw the lowest monthly total at 26,204.
Throughout the year, Ukrainian drone units have consistently inflicted tens of thousands of casualties on Russian forces each month. Monthly totals exceeded 30,000 in January, March, April, May, July, and September.
In September alone, drone strikes killed or wounded 32,739 Russian troops. During the first 25 days of October, Ukrainian forces recorded an additional 27,829 Russian personnel casualties from drone operations.
Overall, as of October 29, 2026, Russia’s estimated personnel losses since the beginning of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine had reached approximately 1,584,910, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.

articles.title: Firehawk raises $150M at $1.4B valuation to build more rocket motors
articles.body:
- Firehawk raised more than $150 million in a Series D led by Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, valuing the company above $1.4 billion.
- The funds will expand its Oklahoma propellant plant and Mississippi missile integration site to scale rocket and artillery motor production.
Dallas-based rocket propulsion firm Firehawk has raised more than $150 million in a Series D round that values the company at more than $1.4 billion, money it will use to scale up U.S. production of rocket propellant, solid rocket motors and artillery motors, the company said on social media on Oct. 28.
Private equity firm Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, co-founded by Dallas investor Kyle Bass, led the round, with new and existing investors and strategic partners also taking part. Firehawk said the round was upsized and oversubscribed, and the Dallas Morning News reported its original target was $100 million. The company did not disclose how much each investor put in.
The money will fund the build-out of Firehawk’s propellant and rocket motor plant in Lawton, Oklahoma, and its missile integration facility in Crawford, Mississippi, along with new research and development sites and more hiring, the company said in its funding announcement. Firehawk plans to produce more than 100,000 artillery motors in 2027 under a commercial agreement with General Dynamics, and its Oklahoma plant is expected to start low-rate production by mid-2027.
Firehawk was founded in 2019 by CEO Will Edwards to make hybrid rocket engines powered by 3D-printed fuel, and it now describes itself as covering the whole chain from propellant to motors to complete rounds. Its pitch is volume: the U.S. military’s appetite for rockets and missiles has outrun the small number of established solid rocket motor suppliers, and Firehawk says its patented manufacturing process can produce propellant faster and at larger scale for smaller tactical weapons.
The company broke ground on its Great Plains Arsenal rocket motor and propellant plant in Lawton in April. Its Crawford site can integrate 40,000 tactical rockets a year, and Firehawk says it plans to raise that to about 120,000 at full-rate production.
Much of that work centers on the Hydra-70, the 70 mm unguided rocket fired from U.S. Army attack helicopters and other aircraft. This summer the U.S. Army picked Firehawk as one of four new companies to build Hydra-70 rockets, alongside iRocket, Nammo Perry and Albers, with each required to deliver 24 prototype M151 rockets within 18 months. In August, Firehawk fired six Hydra-70 rockets at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, all of which worked as intended.
The Series D follows a $60 million Series C that closed in September 2025 and a strategic investment in November 2025 aimed at speeding up solid rocket motor production and integration.
Firehawk has not said how many Hydra-70 rockets or rocket motors it has delivered to the U.S. military so far, or when its Oklahoma plant will reach full-rate production.

articles.title: Your Program Needs Outcomes, Not Outputs
articles.body:
The Department of War is making its acquisition leaders accountable for mission outcomes. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth set the tone in November 2025, when he announced an overhaul of defense acquisition at the National War College. He said contracting officers would be judged on mission outcomes rather than regulatory compliance, and that evaluation criteria would center on mission effectiveness over meeting specifications.
His overhaul also directed the reorganization of program executive offices into portfolio acquisition executives (PAEs), each the single accountable official for the outcomes of an entire portfolio. The strategy released with the overhaul calls for accountability measures that “prioritize outcomes rather than activity.” The Air Force completed its transition in July 2026, designating PAEs for all 17 of its acquisition portfolios.
In September 2026, the DoW CIO brought the same focus to software policy. DoW Instruction 8430.01, Accelerated Mission Software, directs enterprise reporting to focus on value stream and mission outcomes, and treats delivery metrics, like deployment frequency, as diagnostics for individual teams.
Outputs vs. outcomes
Outputs are what a team produces: features, releases, story points, reports. Outcomes are changes in user or system behavior that directly and positively impact the mission value stream. For example, an analyst now completes their task 50% faster, or a pilot now gets the data they need in seconds instead of minutes. Impact is the mission result those changes produce: the mission succeeding, lives saved, critical services reaching the people who need them.
Effort without mission impact
You’ve probably sat through some version of a program review where the team has been at it for months, if not years. They’ve closed hundreds of story points and checked off every milestone, the demos look great, and leadership hears “on track” at every checkpoint. The software makes it to production, but few operators use it, because nobody designed it around how they work. And for all of that effort, the program has made no measurable impact on the mission since the day the government signed the contract.
Unfortunately, this happens to the majority of large government software initiatives. According to the Standish Group data that GSA’s 18F cites, 87% of large government software projects fail. The Standish bar is generous: it counts a project as success when it lands on time, on budget, and with a satisfied customer, even if the mission never changed.
Bryon Kroger, a former Air Force intelligence officer who co-founded Kessel Run (the DoW’s first software factory) and now leads Rise8 as founder and CEO, described programs like these at Prodacity, Rise8’s annual training event for GovTech leaders. He was clear that the people on those programs work hard, contractors and government alike. The problem, he said, is that “the entire system is oriented around the activities and the outputs instead of the outcomes.”
Stop paying for hope
For as much as the community talks about outcomes and new directives call for them, contracts still pay for hours and features. Even firm-fixed-price contracts often pay for level of effort. The government pays the contractor for time spent and people assigned whether or not the mission improves. After delivery, programs often hand adoption to another contractor or a government team, so if the software ships and the mission doesn’t move, the government owns that problem. In general, Kroger said, “we’re buying hope.” Programs pay vendors and hope for an outcome in production that turns into mission value, and that’s a risky bet.
How to buy outcomes
In a world where outcomes are the end goal, outputs should stay off the contract. Teams rarely know exactly what to build up front, so a contract that lists outputs almost always gets them wrong. How do you buy outcomes, then?
Buying outcomes works backward from understanding the desired mission impact. Program leadership names that impact, and the government and contractor team work out which change in user or system behavior would produce it and measure where that behavior stands today. That change and its baseline go on contract, and success means that change, measured in production.
Deliver outcomes, guaranteed
An outcome on contract still needs a team built to deliver it. Kroger saw the limits of the software factory model firsthand at Kessel Run. Software factories brought agile delivery into government, but over time, bureaucracy pulled many of them back to contracts that paid for effort and metrics that counted outputs. What was missing was a model for outcomes from start to finish.
Rise8 built the Outcome Factory to keep what worked and hold every stage accountable to validated mission outcomes. For programs where the government and Rise8 each meet a set of shared commitments, Rise8 guarantees the first validated mission outcome in production within 180 days, or keeps working for free until it is.
The Rise8 Outcome Factory starts with the long-range impact a program needs, maps the current state, and finds the single bottleneck limiting that impact. Together, the Rise8 and government teams set a measurable target aimed at that constraint and continuously deliver software every week until they can validate each outcome against its baseline. When they hit the target, they find the next constraint and start again.
Ask what changed
The Department of War is working to close the gap between outputs and outcomes, from how it judges contracting officers to how it measures software. Every contract can help close this gap too, by naming the change it’s paying for.
The next time a program review says “on track,” ask: what changed for the people using the software, and by how much? If nobody can answer that, the program is still buying outputs and it may be time to start buying outcomes with the Rise8 Outcome Factory. articles.title: Alaska Governor Orders Probe Into Peltola Campaign Over Alleged Spoiler Scheme
articles.body:
Alaska’s Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign following a report that her team helped recruit candidates to draw votes from her Republican opponent, including a man with the same name.
The announcement, posted on social media overnight, followed President Donald Trump’s call for Peltola’s prosecution and escalated Republican efforts to challenge her candidacy just days before an election that could help determine control of the Senate.
On Thursday, Trump declined to say whether Peltola should be seated if she won. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” he told reporters before leaving for a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
Peltola is challenging Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan in the Nov. 3 election. Another candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, has denied running at Democrats’ behest. Alaska’s Supreme Court upheld his eligibility for the ballot earlier this year.
The dispute intensified Wednesday after a New York Times report found that Peltola's team worked with people to recruit men named Dan Sullivan to run for Senate, as well as other candidates who could draw votes away from the incumbent.
Dunleavy said the reporting provided new evidence of an effort to mislead voters and supported state election officials’ earlier findings about Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy.
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” the governor wrote.
Peltola, a former congresswoman, dismissed the report, arguing that it diverted attention from issues including the incumbent Sullivan’s support for the war in Iran.
“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” she said during a campaign stop in Soldotna on Wednesday. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”
A spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign, Alaskans for Mary, said in an email to TIME that it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” The campaign also said it had made no assertions in federal court about how Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy came about or who was involved in his decision to run. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), which was also reportedly involved in the plan, told TIME in a statement that it was “not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.”
Vice President JD Vance also backed an investigation Thursday, accusing Peltola of trying to mislead voters about her campaign’s involvement. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful,” he told reporters before a campaign trip to Texas.
Trump had accused Peltola and her campaign of voter fraud in a series of Truth Social posts Wednesday, calling for her removal from the ballot and prosecution.
“It was just determined that the Dumocrats in Alaska, despite their sworn statements to the contrary, put a man named Dan Sullivan on the Ballot in order to confuse the Public with respect to Highly Esteemed Senator Dan Sullivan,” Trump posted. “This is Voter Fraud at the Highest Level, and the Dumocrat Candidate, who was involved in the scheme, Mary Peltola, should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted—So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan. Nothing else will do!”
The Times noted that ballot-stacking tactics are generally considered legal and have been used by both parties.
At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department had already filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the election results under specific conditions if Senator Sullivan loses, citing the potential for “voter confusion.” The department wants the results recalculated as though votes for Daniel J. Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, and certification blocked if that would change the outcome.
TIME reached out to the Justice Department for comment on how the report affects its case. Attorney General Todd Blanche told Fox News on Wednesday that he expected to “hear more” from the department this week as officials receive new information.
“They are cheating,” Blanche said. “They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues, but by putting up a person with the same name, so that confuses Alaskans.”
What Peltola’s campaign reportedly did
According to the Times’ report, which was based on interviews, text messages, and documents prepared for a possible lawsuit, the Peltola campaign pursued a project known internally as “ballot composition,” which involved campaign lawyers and senior aides at the DSCC, which directs Democratic campaign strategy for Senate races nationwide.
One of the Times’ sources, Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager who was fired during an August staff shake-up, said the operation to recruit potential spoiler candidates for the Alaska ballot began in the summer of 2025. The Times reported that Peltola’s campaign worked with a “veteran Democratic operative” named Jerid Kurtz, whom it described as having expertise in ballot maneuvering.
The Times reported that a Peltola staffer received instructions to “find as many people named Dan Sullivan in Alaska” as possible. Kurtz reportedly found a man in Petersburg named Dan Sullivan who was open to running for Senate.
Rios said Peltola wasn’t directly involved in the project but was “definitely aware.” The Times also reported that Rios later wanted to recant her statements but did not explain why.
Alaska has a nonpartisan primary system, in which voters may choose a candidate regardless of party affiliation, and the top four advance to the general election. Voters then rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins an initial majority, the lowest-ranking candidates are eliminated in successive rounds and their ballots transfer to voters’ next remaining choices.
The spoiler candidate tactic isn’t new
Alaska’s other Senator, Lisa Murkowski, who endorsed Sullivan but supported Peltola years ago, issued a statement Wednesday demanding that Peltola tell the “honest truth” about the apparent ballot-stacking effort.
“While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process,” Murkowski wrote. “Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments. By contrast, recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong.”
Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sullivan’s campaign, also said in a statement that “not one player in this operation has acted in good faith with Alaska voters.”
Republicans have also used similar ballot-stacking tactics. In this year’s Alaska primary, a GOP-aligned political action committee reportedly spent money to boost left-leaning fringe candidates in an attempt to pull votes from Peltola.
When Peltola ran for re-election to the House in 2024, Alaska’s Republican Party supported an effort to help a federally imprisoned Democrat who had never lived in Alaska stay on the ballot.
A GOP-linked political action committee also spent over $1 million this election cycle to boost a third-party candidate in Ohio in a bid to undermine former Senator Sherrod Brown’s comeback bid.
In Minnesota in 2020, Legal Marijuana Now Party candidate Adam Weeks told a close friend before his death that he was recruited by unnamed Republicans to pull votes away from Democrats.

articles.title: How US sanctions are threatening political dissent in Europe
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How US sanctions are threatening political dissent in Europe
The United States is increasingly using its financial power to target political organisations beyond its borders, with consequences extending far into Europe. Under the banner of counterterrorism, US sanctions can effectively cut activists and organisations off from banking services, digital infrastructure, and the financial resources needed to operate, even when European authorities have not designated them as terrorist groups.
The case of Autistici/Inventati (A/I), an Italian digital network providing services to antifascist and anticapitalist organisations, illustrates how this works.
On 26 August 2026, the Trump administration sanctioned A/I alongside the British activist group Palestine Action and the transnational Palestinian organisation Masar Badil. Washington accused them of supporting terrorism, as part of a broader campaign against what it describes as violent far-left extremism.
A/I was designated a Specially Designated Global Terrorist by the US Treasury, which accused it of providing digital infrastructure and services to violent extremist organisations. The collective rejected the accusations, insisting that its work consisted of providing secure communications and digital services to political movements.
Yet the US decision's consequences were felt almost immediately in Italy.
A/I's bank, Banca Etica, suspended operations on its account because of the potential risks associated with US sanctions. The collective also reported disruptions to its website and payment services, eventually announcing that it would dissolve and wind down its activities.
The episode raises a troubling question: how can a decision taken in Washington effectively undermine the operations of organisations based in Europe, without any equivalent decision by European authorities?
Instruments of political pressure
For the European Legal Support Centre (ELSC), an organisation providing legal assistance to individuals and groups mobilising for Palestine, A/I's experience represents a dangerous precedent "that puts the very notion of Europe at risk.”
The case's significance extends beyond A/I itself. It exposes how international financial networks, banking compliance requirements and the threat of US penalties can become instruments of political pressure across national borders.
The US government argues that its sanctions target organisations providing support for terrorism, including violent attacks and damage to property. But the expanding use of counterterrorism measures against activist networks also raises questions about where political dissent ends, and terrorism begins, and who has the power to decide.
The very label of “terrorist” carries a long history of political use - which dates back to the British Empire - and appears to be applied selectively. The legal distinctions matter. A US sanctions designation is not a criminal conviction, nor does it automatically make an organisation illegal under European law. Nevertheless, the practical consequences can be devastating.
For banks and financial institutions that depend on access to USA financial networks, the risk of maintaining relations with a sanctioned organisation may simply be considered too great. This creates a system in which European organisations can face financial and social exclusion because of decisions made by a foreign government, even without direct legal orders from their own authorities.
The case of Mohammad Hannoun, a Palestinian activist based in Italy, demonstrates another dimension of this pressure. Hannoun faced restrictions on his banking activities before the US government sanctioned him in October 2024 over allegations relating to Hamas financing. Italian authorities subsequently detained him amid criminal proceedings alleging he funded the group.
Hannoun's case involves separate criminal allegations and judicial proceedings, which should not be confused with the sanctions themselves. Nevertheless, it illustrates how financial restrictions, political accusations and legal proceedings can intersect.
These developments reflect a wider system in which state authorities, banks, media organisations, universities, cultural venues, and lawfare groups can collectively contribute to isolating individuals, groups, and networks accused of supporting terrorism.
The impact on solidarity efforts
The implications are particularly concerning for activists and organisations supporting Palestine, whose activities have faced increasing scrutiny and restrictions in several European countries. In Britain, Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025 following its direct-action campaign against companies connected to Israel's defence industry. The group has challenged the ban in court, with the UK Supreme Court due to hear an appeal in November 2026.
The subsequent US designation of Palestine Action illustrates how one government's measures can be reinforced by another, potentially multiplying their impact on the organisations concerned.
But the A/I case points to something further: extending such measures to organisations that provide services and infrastructure used by political movements.
The question is whether European institutions have either the tools or the political willingness to challenge this expanding extraterritorial reach.
The European Union does possess a legal mechanism intended to protect European individuals and businesses against certain foreign sanctions: the Blocking Statute, introduced under Council Regulation (EC) No 2271/96. Originally adopted in 1996, the statute was designed to counter the effects of US sanctions on European economic operators. It was subsequently updated in 2018 in response to the reimposition of US sanctions against Iran.
The legislation can prohibit compliance with specified foreign sanctions and provide legal remedies to affected European operators. However, it applies only to the foreign legislation covered by its annex, which currently includes certain US measures concerning Cuba and Iran. It does not automatically protect organisations targeted under the US counterterrorism sanctions regime.
Extending or adapting such protections would require further action by European institutions, and would not necessarily eliminate the financial risks facing European banks.
Nevertheless, this legal mechanism shows that the EU has previously recognised the problem posed by the extraterritorial application of US sanctions.
As the ELSC pointed out: "We have this European law, but it has never been used on the scale required to counter the US sanctions."
The consequences of inaction are not merely financial. When an organisation loses access to its bank accounts, online services or funding channels, its ability to operate can rapidly disappear. The threat of sanctions can also discourage other organisations, financial institutions, and individuals from associating with it, even before any formal restrictions are imposed.
"The aim of the US sanctions is to isolate and fragment the European political movement for Palestine," the ELSC argued. "A sanctioned person will be concerned about how to recover funds instead of doing their work."
These chilling effects are difficult to measure, but they are central to understanding the wider implications of the sanctions regime. In the A/I case, the collective's decision to dissolve shows how legal uncertainty, financial pressure, and risk to associated individuals can make the situation unsustainable.
The European Union frequently presents itself as a defender of civil liberties, the rule of law and political freedoms. Yet these commitments face a practical test when European organisations are subjected to financial restrictions originating outside their own legal system.
The question is not whether organisations accused of terrorism should be exempt from scrutiny. Rather, the question is whether European institutions should allow foreign sanctions decisions, and the financial pressure they generate, to determine whether organisations operating within Europe can survive.
If the consequences of a US designation can effectively shut down a European organisation without an equivalent decision under European law, the boundary between US financial power and European political sovereignty becomes increasingly difficult to distinguish.
For European civil society, that boundary may be far more important than it first appears.

articles.title: Human rights commissioner explains how residents will be evacuated from occupied Oleshky
articles.body:
Human rights commissioner explains how residents will be evacuated from occupied Oleshky
Under an agreement reached by the Russian and Ukrainian sides, the evacuation route for residents of Oleshky will pass through Russia and Belarus before reaching Ukraine.
Source: Lubinets, Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsman), on social media; Ukrainian Ombudsman's Office
Quote from Lubinets: "I am still on my way to Oleshky. Our humanitarian mission is ongoing.
I can see that people on social media are already writing that I am on Russian territory. There are many questions and provocative posts appearing.
So I want to explain: I'm going there to be on the ground in person, see what is happening and keep you informed about the progress of the mission."
Details: The ombudsman urged people not to jump to conclusions.
"You cannot even imagine how difficult these negotiations have been, or how long they took to make sure that I am here, where I am now. But we have only covered half the distance towards achieving our goal. So I ask you to please leave all questions until I return home," Lubinets added.
Earlier, US broadcaster Fox News published a document signed by Russian ombudsman Yana Lantratova, which stated that residents of Oleshky who wished to evacuate to Ukraine would first be taken to the airport in the city of Anapa in Russia's Krasnodar Krai.
From Anapa, the Ukrainian delegation and residents of Oleshky will be transported to the airport in the city of Gomel in Belarus aboard a Russian Defence Ministry military transport aircraft. This is likely to take place on Saturday 31 October.
The Ukrainian ombudsman's office stressed that the document was not a military or political agreement.
"When human lives are at stake, saving people and achieving tangible results must come first, rather than political assessments. The temporarily occupied territories are part of Ukraine. A humanitarian mission must not become hostage to information manipulation," the statement said.
"The situation around Oleshky is unprecedented. We are doing something that has not previously been achieved in this format: seeking a way to save people who need help. We thank US First Lady Melania Trump for her assistance, coordination and concern for the fate of these people.
We therefore urge people not to create a sense of 'betrayal' where unity is needed. It is now very important to support the Ukrainian delegation and keep our fingers crossed for a successful outcome," Lubinets's office also stressed.
Previously: On 29 October, Lubinets and a delegation set off directly for the area of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky, Kherson Oblast. His Russian counterpart, Lantratova, also said she was heading there.
Background:
- Lubinets announced that a ceasefire in the Oleshky area had started at 03:00 on 27 October. Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed that the ceasefire had been introduced.
- Earlier, the White House announced that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine in the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky, where a humanitarian disaster is currently unfolding.
- The ceasefire is due to remain in effect until 22:59 on 1 November.

articles.title: Hackers expose US immigration surveillance network
articles.body:
Hackers expose US immigration surveillance network
Personal and operational details of more than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors, including undercover immigration agents, have been leaked online, reportedly exposing the department’s internal structure and surveillance operations.
The disclosure comes amid growing public anger over President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign, with the department’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facing growing criticism over aggressive raids, detention conditions, and the use of force against migrants and protesters.
Released on Wednesday by transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), the files contain names, contact details, job titles, and internal system access groups across ICE, Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and other DHS agencies.
DHS confirmed to the media that it is “aware of a potential breach” and is working to address it, adding that it will protect employees and update the public “when more information is available.”
What’s in the files?
Dubbed ‘Icepick’, the archive was supplied to DDoSecrets by a hacktivist group called ‘Department of Peace’. It contains around 21,300 CBP records, 6,600 linked to ICE, and 3,400 to Homeland Security Investigations, along with records from immigration services, cybersecurity, and other DHS divisions. Some records match employees’ social media profiles, but others exposed internal organizational charts and previously undisclosed programs and operations.
According to Wired, the files reference undercover investigations, wiretapping, and immigration databases, with internal access groups linked to surveillance tools including Palantir’s Falcon software and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition system used by immigration agents. Other groups reference AI services including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Elon Musk’s xAI chatbot Grok. Access groups are lists of employees authorized to use particular systems, which means the records could help identify which employees have access to surveillance tools and how DHS operations are organized.
“This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” investigative journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew, who developed a searchable version of the archive, said in a statement accompanying the release. She called it “a complete game changer for anyone investigating DHS,” arguing that it could help identify agents and their chains of command.
DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said the files go beyond an ordinary employee directory.
“Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations,” she said, pointing to officials overseeing covert investigations, efforts to identify government leakers, and deportation programs.
The hackers claim to have obtained the records through DHS’s Okta employee login system, though Okta denied that its systems were compromised.
Why now?
The hackers linked the leak to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s pledge to intensify immigration enforcement. Speaking after two fatal ICE shootings in Texas and Maine, Mullin said federal agents are “turning up the heat on the streets,” despite growing criticism of their tactics. “On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ‘turning up the heat.’ This is what happens to ICE when you do that,” a Department of Peace spokesperson said in a statement published by DDoSecrets.
The disclosure comes amid growing backlash over Trump’s immigration crackdown, a central priority since his return to the White House in January 2025. His push for mass deportations, expanded detention, and tighter border controls has sparked protests over aggressive raids, masked agents, and alleged racial profiling.
Anger intensified after federal agents fatally shot US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota in January, followed by other violent incidents involving ICE officers. Just this month, federal agents shot and wounded a Dominican migrant during an arrest in New York, prompting further demonstrations.
ICE has also faced scrutiny over detention conditions, with at least 52 deaths in its custody during Trump’s first 500 days back in office, according to Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights.
The administration maintains that its operations are necessary to enforce immigration law and remove dangerous criminals. The Icepick publishers say the records can help journalists, lawmakers, and civil liberties groups investigate DHS activities. Emma Best argued that the disclosure can enable investigations, congressional inquiries, and legal challenges by replacing the administration’s “anonymity with accountability.”
Yet another breach
The disclosure adds to a series of US government data security incidents.
In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed that it stole personal data on nearly all FBI agents and their spouses, including sensitive job details and medical information. The group said the attack was “not financially motivated” and demanded that the FBI withdraw a cybersecurity advisory published in May that it claimed contained false allegations about it.
Separately, a Pentagon personnel system breach reportedly exposed Social Security numbers, personal details, and military job records belonging to more than 3 million people, including service members and their families. The incident prompted a class-action lawsuit last week.
